s01.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 6 · 4:45 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: The alarm on the windowsill is a bright little run of marimba, cheerful as a game show, and Jack sleeps through it exactly as advertised. What wakes him is the rain. It’s on the shingles, fine and steady, and running in the gutter at the corner of the window, and under it, close by, there’s the sound of a zipper being done up slowly so as not to wake anybody.

She’s dressing in the dark by the gray that comes in around the curtain from the corner streetlight. Jeans. His flannel from the Walk, buttoned to the throat. The sheepskin coat over it, the big collar turned up. He watches her through his eyelashes and doesn’t let on, and she hums a little for her audience without turning around.

At the closet she reaches up to the shelf and takes down the hat. She stands there holding it by the brim in both hands, turning it a little in the gray, a while. She lays it back on the shelf, crown down, where it was.
She opens the desk drawer, drops something in it that clinks, and bumps the drawer shut with her hip.
“Key’s in the drawer,” she says. “Start her twice a week. She sulks.”
“Who sulks.”
“The *car*, Youngstown.”

He’s asleep again before she’s finished laughing at him, or near enough. What comes next is headlights sliding across the ceiling. He lifts his head off the pillow. Through the gap in the curtain there’s a town car at the bottom of Sol’s porch steps, black and shining, its wipers going, and a driver under an umbrella with his hand already on the back door like he’s holding it for a bride.

The suitcase goes down the stairs first. He hears every step of it with his eyes shut — the bump, the bump, the wheels catching on the landing, the driver at the bottom saying *I got it, I got it*. She comes back up for the carry-on, and for him.

She kneels on the mattress in the coat. The sheepskin is cold from the open door downstairs and smells like rain. She kisses him the way she said she would, slow, taking her time over it like there’s no car at all, one hand spread open on his chest over the CREW sweatshirt. Her thumb moves on the lettering. She sits back on her heels with her eyebrows up and waits for *mm*.

The front door. The car door, a heavy, expensive sound in the rain.

Then it’s Skye, laughing on every stair to the bottom, and the front door, and the car door shutting on the rain.

response: She stops in the doorway with her hand on the frame. In the gray he can see her mouth and not much else.
“That’s the plan,” she says.
Her hand taps the frame twice. “Wash the sweatshirt.”
The stairs. The car door.

body: He sleeps through the taillights. He wakes at ten in her bed with the rain stopped and the window gone white, in the CREW sweatshirt, which he was told to wash and has now slept in twice, and which he will tell her he washed. Her side of the mattress is cold. In the desk drawer the Saab key lies on a Sweetwater call sheet folded in four, and he takes the key, and the hat off her closet shelf, crown down, and leaves the Saab where it is, nosed in at the curb with the rain standing on its hood in beads. Del Playa after weather: the gutters still running, the bluff stairs dark with wet, the kelp coming up off the beach as the sun gets to it.

412 empty is a different room. Theo’s bed is made with hospital corners. The camel coat is gone off the desk chair. The DVD stack stands where Theo left it, every case with its yellow Post-it in fountain pen, FRI on top, already a day behind. Jack sits at Theo’s desk with the RAZR open and reads Skye’s morning in the order it came.

s02a.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 6 · 3:20 PM · OCEAN ROAD → 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412
body: It comes in the afternoon, in the room. He’s on the edge of his own bed with Fenner’s problem set on his knee, and the fourth floor is so quiet he can hear the pop machine humming at the end of the hall. The sweatshirt’s cuffs are chewed through at the thumbs. Over the footlocker the crucifix hangs where it has hung since August, and he has been sitting under it for twenty minutes without looking up, and when he notices that, he still can’t look up.

It’s the size of the room. Last night is in his body like the heat in a stone after the sun’s gone, and it was good — he won’t let anybody tell him it wasn’t, himself first — and it’s also what it is, and he knew what it was when he asked her, and he asked her. Both of those are in 412 with him. Neither one leaves to make room for the other.

St. Brendan’s hears confessions Saturdays at three-thirty. By twenty past he’s on Ocean Road in the Carhartt with his hands in the pockets, and his feet know the way. The courtyard gate is open. The side door is propped with the cast-iron doorstop shaped like a duck, and through it he can see the card table and somebody’s purse on a folding chair.

He keeps walking. Past the gate, past the olive tree, down the hill to where Ocean Road quits and the bluff path starts, to the rail above the water, where there’s nothing to do but stand. His legs won’t take the turn, and he knows exactly why, and he doesn’t tell himself anything else about it: not that he’s tired, not that it’s too soon, not that Osei will be there next week. He stands at the rail with the kelp beds going brown and gold below him and the shame sitting in his face like a sunburn, and the three-thirty hour goes by behind him, up the hill, without him.

body.text: Skye’s sentence comes back to him in her voice, in the coat, close enough not to touch: *Go back Saturday. I’ll be on a plane. Nothing will be in the way.* It’s Saturday. She’s on a mountain in New Mexico. Nothing is.
Osei’s voice, from Wednesday: *one Wednesday, to see you come up this hill from somewhere else.* He has come from somewhere else. He’s going down the hill from it.

Going past, he saw the little bulb in its wire cage over the closet door, through the blue glass, unlit, because it’s Saturday and the bulb is a Wednesday thing. He walked past it Wednesday too, when it was on.

body: He works his Saturday at the Anchor, seven to one, at the Hobart with his sleeves wet to the elbow. Gloria asks him nothing all night. Gloria asks everybody everything.

body: It comes off the case at twenty to two and sticks to his thumb, a night late. *The Third Man*, on Theo’s MacBook, on his knees, in the dark. The zither starts before the picture does and hardly stops for two hours, and he hates it by the end of the first reel, as advertised. A writer of cowboy paperbacks comes to Vienna to find a friend, and the city is rubble cut into four pieces, and the friend is worse than dead.

Then the last shot, which he was told to wait for, and he waits. A long road through a cemetery in winter, straight as a rule, bare trees down both sides of it and the leaves still coming down. A man waits by a cart at the side of the road. Far off, down the middle, a woman is walking toward the camera. She takes a long time to get there. She comes level with him and goes past him and doesn’t turn her head, and keeps walking, and the camera holds on the road until she’s gone out of the side of the picture. The man lights a cigarette. He throws the match away.
The zither comes up over THE END. Jack shuts the laptop.

s03.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 7 · 9:00 AM · THE OLD MISSION, NUESTRA SEÑORA DEL MAR
body: The sun is on the Mission’s front by nine, warm on the old whitewash and the two bells in their arches, and the steps are still dark from somebody’s hose. It’s three miles from St. Brendan’s. Inside it’s cool and low and dim, beeswax and floor polish and the perfume of women who have been coming to the nine o’clock since Eisenhower.

He doesn’t know a soul here, and not one of them knows him. That’s why he came. Old women in the front pews with lace on their heads; a family of six in a row by height; a baby on its father’s shoulder, looking back at Jack over a pressed white shirt with an expression of complete judgment. Through the wall the choir for the ten-thirty is running a Spanish hymn in pieces, stopping and starting over. He sits on the left, halfway back, which is not where he sat in December.

The Gospel is Luke, and it finds him anyway. Simon has been out all night and caught nothing. A carpenter climbs into his boat and tells a fisherman where the fish are, and Simon, who knows better, lets the nets down, and the nets start to tear and the boats start to go under, and Simon goes down on his knees in a pile of fish and says it: *“Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.”*

The priest reads the next verse. Jack doesn’t hear it. He’s still in the boat with Simon on his knees in the catch, with the line Simon said, the line Jack would say, and he stays there while the priest reads on to the end and kisses the book. The priest is old, Mexican-American, with a voice that has done this ten thousand times and never performed it, and he preaches a short one on the nets. Jack comes back for one sentence. “Simon was the expert. He had already done everything right. That is the worst time to be told where the fish are.”

At Communion the pew empties around him and the line goes up the center aisle past his knees, slow, shuffling, a hundred people who know what they’re doing. He stays in the pew. He kneels — kneeling is allowed — and looks at the back of the pew in front of him, where somebody cut a small cross into the wood a long time ago and somebody else varnished over it. Nobody here knows to notice he doesn’t go. That’s the point, and it doesn’t help.
He’s out the side door before the recessional, into sun hard enough to make him squint, and behind the wall the choir starts its hymn again from the top.

journal.title: Doug Pruitt
journal.text: Doug Pruitt. 420, with Kevin. Bakersfield. Mechanical engineering. A Tauren druid. Says ‘dude’ with five vowels. Tuesday the 8th, 3:58 in the morning, I caught his wrist on the east-stair pull station. He was asleep. The raid boss was in the elevator. Super Bowl Sunday on his futon with Yusuf, the surround sound wired for the island and now for this. He stood up on the futon for the onside kick. When Theo called from the street he screamed *who dat* into my phone and New Orleans screamed it back.

body: At 3:02 the sun comes through the window of 420 at the one angle that defeats a television, and Doug has beaten it with a bedsheet, a roll of duct tape and four hours of conviction.

The Logitech is up. Five speakers on a long sagging loop of wire are duct-taped along the bookshelf on Kevin’s half of the room. The rest of his half is untouched: the bed made tight enough to bounce a quarter, the label maker, an orgo flowchart in a plastic sleeve. On Kevin’s pillow there’s an index card he left Friday morning, *DISCLOSURE: I HAVE NOT AUTHORIZED THIS*, and under it, in Doug’s marker, *dude it sounds amazing*.
Doug is in a black Brees jersey with the Big 5 fold lines still across the chest. “For solidarity,” he says, when Jack looks. “With who?” “Dude. Everybody.”

The futon sags in the middle like a hammock somebody gave up on. The frame came out of the fourth-floor lounge and the mattress out of a donation bin, and Jack carried the heavy end, which in moral theology makes him a cooperator in evil, remote and material. Yusuf is on the floor with his back against it and a legal pad on his knee, on which he has drawn the field and cut it into zones he declines to explain.
The RAZR goes off against Jack’s hip as he sits.

“The Colts.” Jack takes a handful of Doug’s chips. “They left Baltimore in the middle of the night in Mayflower vans. In Ohio we know what it means when the vans come at night.”
“Duuude,” says Doug, with feeling, and settles in to hate Indianapolis.

By the end of the first quarter the Colts are up 10–0, and Doug has said *It’s fine* so many times that it has stopped being a sentence. “It’s *fine*,” he says. “It’s a first-pull wipe. You don’t disband the raid.” He looks over at Jack for the first time since the coin toss. “Dude, you look like you slept in a bus station.”
“I’m good.”
“Cool.” Yusuf glances up from the pad and back down, and draws a line.

The second half opens with the Saints lining up to kick off, and something is wrong with the formation, and Doug says “They’re not—” and they are. The ball squibs ten yards and disappears under a pile of men in black and gold and white, and the referee digs through it, and comes up pointing the Saints’ way. Doug is on the futon, on his feet, and the frame makes a sound like a car accident and holds.
“That is insane,” says Yusuf, who has put down the pen, with something near reverence. “They removed the factor of safety. On purpose. At kickoff.”
Jack is up too, both hands on top of his head, standing on Doug’s rug in his socks and yelling at the Super Bowl.

With three minutes left, and 420 gone quiet enough to hear the subwoofer breathing, Peyton Manning throws for the sideline and Tracy Porter is simply there, as if he’d been issued the ball, and takes it all the way back with the fourth floor behind him.
“Single point of failure,” Yusuf says, not looking up from the pad.
Doug is no longer on the futon. He’s on the rug, face down, screaming into it. Saints 31, Colts 17, and the last minutes are a formality that the three of them watch to the end anyway.

body: Yusuf tears the top sheet off the legal pad, folds it in four, and puts it in his shirt pocket. “For the record,” he says, “the zones were wrong.” Doug leans down over the back of the futon and hugs him around the neck, and Yusuf allows it for the length of one breath.

The RAZR rings at 7:09, THEO VANCE (IMPORTANT) across the little screen, and Jack opens it a foot from his ear and the city comes out. Horns, hundreds of them, no two on the same note. A brass band somewhere off the phone’s left shoulder, tuba first, moving. A stranger leans into Theo’s phone and screams *WHO DAT*, and Doug, who has crossed the room without being asked, screams it back into the RAZR from six inches, and the stranger screams it back again, hoarse and joyful, at a boy in a dormitory he will never meet.
“Costigan.” Theo, over all of it. “Are you hearing this? This is a city that has been told no for forty-three years.” Forty-three years is three more than the Israelites got, and they had a cloud.

response: Theo says nothing, and into the gap goes the brass band, tuba first.
“So am I,” he says. No pitch in it anywhere, none of the cashmere. “Mostly.”
The line fills up with tuba and goes dead.
“You don’t get to say that, Costigan. You’re from *Ohio*. You people say *O-H*.”
“He has a point,” Yusuf says, from the floor.
Theo hangs up into the brass band.

“That’s a call and response,” says Yusuf. “It’s liturgical.”
Jack gets the phone back in time for the dial tone.

s05.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 7 · 10:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM — THE MOTEL
body: *It’s a Wonderful Life* ran till ten in 420, because Doug would not hear of a man watching it alone on the night of the Saints. He cried at the bell. Yusuf studied the ceiling tiles for the length of it.

Machine three is thumping through its spin cycle like it has something to prove. His towels are in it, and his jeans, and every shirt he owns that Theo hasn’t called a cry for help. The sweatshirt isn’t, because he’s wearing it. The Delgado laundry room on a Sunday night is a buzzing tube light, the warm chemical sweetness of a hundred people’s dryer sheets with none of the people, a lost-and-found box of single socks on the folding table, and his RAZR beside the box, ringing.

It’s the first long one. She’s in the motel outside Santa Fe, on the bed in her coat, because the wall heater has to think about it first. “Listen.” He hears it through the phone: a knock, like somebody at a door, and then the roar. “Every time. Like it’s asking permission.” Down the walkway the ice machine drops a load. Out in the lot two grips are arguing about the Colts in the cold, and she does them for him, one from Indianapolis who is taking it personally and one who had twenty dollars on New Orleans and wants it understood that it was a matter of principle.

The table read was this morning, in a church hall in town with folding chairs and a crucifix and a coffee urn that bled onto the tablecloth. “I said *Out*,” she says, “and it had something on it this time. I don’t know what. The room went quiet. The man playing my father — the sheriff — he looked up from his pages, and he didn’t look down again. The whole read. He just watched me.” She lets a breath go into the phone. “Everybody was waiting to see if Cassidy can be anybody else. Me too.”
Jack leans on the folding table with the phone and doesn’t say anything. It isn’t his turn yet.
“And my mother booked the room next door for next week,” she says. “She called the front desk and asked for the connecting key. Like it’s a *suite*.”

body.text: “And you packed me like a *Costigan*. I can’t get one thing out without everything coming out. I wanted a sock and I got Ohio.”
body.else: “I packed myself. Everything I own is in one sock.”

body: She knows the words for it now. She learned them in his car and in his pew, and she uses them carefully, the way she’d hold somebody else’s good camera.
“Did you go up today?”

choices.text: “No. I went to Mass in town and stayed in the pew.”
response: “In *town*.”
“At the Mission.”
“You’re hiding from your priest.”
“For a week.”
“I hid from my mother for two years once. On a soundstage.” The heater roars along behind her. “They always find you at the craft-services table.”
Outside her door the grips have gone in. What’s left is the ice machine and her breathing, close to the phone.
“Go back Wednesday.”
Down the walkway the ice machine drops its whole load, and she waits till it’s done.
“Okay,” she says. “Then I’m coming home.”

She tells him about the grips instead. The Indianapolis one has gone to sit in his truck with the engine running, and the other one is doing a touchdown dance by himself under the light over the ice machine, slow, in a parka, with his arms up, for an audience of one bucket. She narrates it like golf, low and reverent, until Jack has to sit down on the folding table.

A sorrel mare named Clementine, who doesn’t like anybody and likes Skye least of all, and on the first afternoon stood on the wrangler’s foot and went on standing on it to make a point. The wrangler is a slow man from Española with a voice like a gravel driveway: “*She ain’t mean. She’s particular.*” The horse is mostly a long wet sigh through the lips, and Skye’s is good enough that Jack looks over his shoulder at the dryers.
At the end of the horse she moves the phone to her other ear.
“You didn’t answer me.”
He keeps the phone at his ear and lets her have that.
“Night, Jack.”
Machine three buzzes.

body: A picture message follows, and it builds all the way down the salad bar: a bar in lamplight, a squat glass, something amber, a twist of peel on the rim. No caption. Theo has never in his life sent a picture without a caption; he captions weather. Jack reads the text twice and the picture once and answers neither.

Afternoon, and he starts the Saab at the curb on Del Playa, because he was told twice a week and it has been three days. It stalls pulling out. It stalls again at the foot of Sol’s steps, and on the porch Tomás, wet-haired, in from the water, with a mug, has gone still in his chair to watch. The third time it catches, runs rough for a block, and then doesn’t.
Tomás lifts the mug as Jack rolls past. “She was sulking.”

s06a.slug: TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 9 · 11:52 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE BACK LOT — SNOW
body: His break is ten minutes behind the dumpster corral, by the propane cage, in a wet apron, with steam coming off his forearms into the cold. It’s the only spot behind the Anchor where the RAZR finds its bar. Through the screen door the Hobart is going like a train in a tunnel, out past the lot the freeway hisses on wet pavement, and the phone rings in his hand.
“It’s snowing,” Skye says. “Jack. It’s *snowing*. Listen.”
He listens. He gets nothing at all — no heater, no ice machine, no grips — and takes the phone away from his ear to check the bars.
“That’s it,” he tells her. “That’s what it sounds like.”

“I’ve been in snow. Snow at a lodge at Christmas, from inside, with cocoa. Paper snow on a soundstage that gets in your bra.” Her voice goes up, like her face has gone up with it. “I’ve never stood in it while it *came down*. It’s landing on me. It doesn’t weigh anything.”

Jack laughs at her, a Youngstown laugh, a laugh with a few hundred driveways in it — and stops, because she’s gone quiet on the other end, and he can see her without trying: the coat, the motel lot, her face tipped up into it with her mouth open.

So he tells her what snow is for. It’s for Mrs. DeLuca’s walk on Glenwood, five dollars and a Coke, and she checks the corners with her cane. It’s for the hill at Mill Creek above the lily pond, where half the South Side goes on a snow day with cafeteria trays and garbage-can lids and one kid every year on an inner tube who finds the tree. It’s for Danny, eleven years old, pulling him up that hill on a flattened Giant Eagle box with a clothesline through it, and down, and up again, until the box went soft and gave out in the slush, and then Danny carrying him the rest of the way home on his back, both of them soaked through, Danny saying *you weigh a thousand pounds* every block and not putting him down.
There’s a sound on her end like a coat going down onto a sidewalk.
“What are you doing?”
“Lying in it,” she says. “In your flannel. In the parking lot. Under the orange light. The night clerk is watching me out the office window like I’m on fire.”

Jack is grinning at a dumpster. He’s standing behind a diner near midnight in a wet apron with his arms steaming, doing it at the phone, at the propane cage, at the sky over the lot where there isn’t any snow, and there’s nobody to see it but a cat on the fence who has seen worse.
The screen door bangs. Rudy, with a spatula: “Costigan. The Hobart.”
“I have to go wash a pie tin,” Jack tells her.
“Go. I’m making an angel.” A crunch, and the coat shushing back and forth. “That’s a Catholic thing, right?”
“It’s a kid thing.”
“In Ohio,” she says, “that’s the same thing.”
Rudy holds the screen door open with his boot and looks at Jack’s face, and at the sky, and lets him by.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 10 · 7:58 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — BACK TO THE LIGHT
body: The bulb is on. He sees it from halfway down Ocean Road, through the blue glass at the back of the nave, a forty-watt in a wire cage, and he keeps his eyes on it the rest of the way down from Delgado so his feet won’t get any ideas. The courtyard is dark. The card table inside the doors is bare. On the closet door the index card still says KNOCK (GENTLY), and the golf pencil hangs under it on its string.
He hasn’t got it ready. He tried, on the walk, and it kept coming out in long sentences with reasons in them, so he quit somewhere around the eucalyptus and decided to bring it in the way it is.
He knocks gently. On the far side the beads stop.

Inside, somebody has fixed the kneeler. The split corner where the yellow foam showed through is mended with gaffer tape, a neat silver X, pressed down hard at the edges by somebody’s thumb. Somebody noticed. He kneels on it.

body.text: “Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been a week.”
“A week.” The chair on the far side takes Osei’s weight. “You came back.”
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been a week.” He says the next part straight. “You absolved me of Sunday.” He breathes. “This is Friday.”
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been two weeks.”
“I know.” The chair takes Osei’s weight. “I saw a man in a Carhartt from the window last Wednesday. I hoped it was you.”

It was my first time.” The tape doesn’t give under his knee the way the foam did. “I asked her. That part’s mine.” He doesn’t dress it up or down. “She left Saturday morning for New Mexico. For work, two weeks.”

“And the Sunday before. Her bed. I never brought it in. I got as far as your steps.”

body: “Saturday I came down here at three-thirty. The gate was open. I kept walking. Sunday I went to Mass in town, where nobody knows me, and I stayed in the pew.” He stops. Osei waits until he’s sure that’s the end of it.
“Thank you,” Osei says.
“For what?”

“For not making it smaller. Or bigger. Men do both in here, Jack. Most of them on the same night.” The chair creaks. “It is a grave thing, and you knew it when you asked her. I will not pretend with you, and you did not come here to be pretended with.” A breath through the linen. “And you came back inside a week. I have waited years for some men. Some of them I am still waiting for.”

body.text: “I asked you once to come up this hill from somewhere else.” Something on the far side of the linen that is a smile, or close to one. “I did not mean New Mexico.”
body.else: “Two Wednesdays and two other doors.” The beads move. “A man can wear out a hill going around it.”

body: Jack takes it. He has it coming.
“Which church?” Osei says.
“The Mission.”
“What did they read you?”
“Luke five. The boats.” He has had the line in his mouth since Sunday, so he gives it over. “*Depart from me, Lord.*”
“And did He?”
Jack opens his mouth and has nothing to put in it. He stopped listening at the fish.
“He said, *Do not be afraid.*” The beads click on the far side. “And He took him along in the boat. Peter said the true thing about himself, and he was told it was not the end of the conversation.”
Jack has the kneeler’s tape under his knee and a question he didn’t bring in with him. “Did it take? With Peter. After the boat.”

“Peter?” The beads stop. “He fell asleep in the garden. He cut off a man’s ear. He said three times he had never met Him, to a serving girl, by a fire.” A pause, not long. “All of that after the fish, and He kept him anyway.”
Somewhere down the hill a freight blows for the crossing at the slough, long and low, and goes on up the coast.

“Pray for her by name,” Osei says. “Every day. For her. Not against her.” The chair creaks. “Not that she will go away, or that you will stop wanting her. What is good in her is God’s, and a man does not run from God’s things. He keeps away from the room and the hour. Pray for Skye’s good. You will learn what it is by asking for it.”
“I have been,” Jack says. “That she gets there. That the horse doesn’t throw her. That the snow holds off till she wants it.”
“Good. That is the beginning of it. Keep going past the weather.”
“Now.” The voice behind the linen is quiet and not soft. “I am not asking what will happen. I am asking what you intend.”

He has two answers again, the true one and the owed one, and he holds them up side by side in the dark like two boards in Pop’s garage that are supposed to come out one length. He measures twice. They don’t.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. St. Blaise: two crossed candles at my throat, and then, for me, eight o’clock. Wednesday night I went in. I told him the song, all of it, and Sunday night. He said I’m not avoiding the near occasion, I’m commuting to it. He didn’t ask me to know the future. He asked what I intend. I told him the truth: I don’t know that I do. He couldn’t absolve me. He blessed me instead. The light’s on Wednesdays, he said. He’ll be there. Wednesday, February tenth, I went back. Four days and two doors first: Saturday’s hour I walked past, and Sunday I went to the Mission in town and stayed in the pew. I told him Friday night, plainly. He asked what they read me at the Mission. *Depart from me, Lord.* And did He? He told Peter not to be afraid, and took him along. Pray for her by name, he said. For her, not against her. Then he asked what I intend. I told him the truth: I can’t promise. A blessing again. Then we will keep meeting, he said. That is also what the chair is for.

Behind the linen, nothing, for as long as it takes the last of the freight to clear the crossing.

s07a.slug: WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 10 · 8:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE BOX
body: “Then make a good act of contrition.”

He says the one from St. Brigid’s, the one with *Thee* in it, that he learned at seven and could say in his sleep by eight. It runs the way it always runs until *to avoid the near occasion of sin*, which sits in his mouth longer than the rest of it, because he knows exactly where the near occasion lives. A room at the bottom of the hill, an hour, a door. It’s standing dark tonight with the Saab at the curb. He says it anyway, all of it, to *Amen*.

On the linen the shadow of Osei’s hand comes up. “…through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins” — the shadow makes its two strokes over him — “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
Something in his chest that has been clenched since Saturday afternoon lets go a notch, the way a fist does in sleep, and he hasn’t done a thing to earn it.

“For your penance: Luke five, every night until Sunday. Out loud. Stop where He says *Do not be afraid*. Not one verse further.” A breath through the linen that has something like a laugh at the bottom of it. “The fish will keep.”
“Thanks be to God.”
“Go in peace, Jack.”
He gets up off the tape. Through his jeans his knee has the X on it, faintly, and he carries it out with him.

s07b.slug: WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 10 · 8:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE BOX
body: Osei answers at once, as if he had the answer ready all week and was sorry to need it.

“Then I cannot absolve you tonight.” No sermon comes after it. “I will not pretend otherwise. I wish I could; absolving is the best part of this chair.” The beads move. “You will have a blessing. That is yours whenever you want it. And you will come back.”
The shadow of his hand comes up on the linen. “May almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
He braced for this on the walk down: the door, the dark, the climb back up the hill with nothing in his hands. Jack waits to be sent out, and instead the chair creaks, a man settling in.

“Then we will keep meeting,” Osei says. “That is also what the chair is for.” The beads go around under his thumb. “Bring me the true thing every week. The true thing is not the whole medicine. It is the part a man can carry up a hill.”
“Is that enough?” Jack says. “The part I can carry.”
“It is enough to come back with.”
“Yes, Father.”
“Good night, Jack.”
He gets up off the tape with a blessing and nothing else, and it weighs what a blessing weighs, which is more than he’d figured. Through his jeans his knee has the X on it, faintly.

Outside the gate the hill goes two ways. Downhill is the way his legs know: Ocean Road to the bottom, Del Playa, a dark house with the Saab at the curb and the porch light off. He turns uphill instead, toward Delgado, and halfway up the RAZR is out of his pocket.

s08.slug: THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 11 – FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 12 · HOLLIS HALL, 302 → THE ANCHOR → THE FISHBOWL
body: The sun reaches the window end of 302 at five past one and lies down the varnish in a bright slab, with the last chair in the middle of it, empty. The table has stopped using that chair out of something like manners: the two window girls have shifted a seat down, Yusuf’s cup keeps to its own end, and Caleb has hung his backpack on the next chair so that the strap makes a velvet rope. It’s a molded beige chair with a gouge in one arm, and it is, Jack decides, the most influential person in the room.
Evan has the roster at the door. Over his head, on the whiteboard, in Hale’s tilted hand: HAPPY BIRTHDAY MR. MARSH — DO NOT SING. Caleb’s mouth is already open on the first syllable.
“Mr. Hargrove,” says Hale, coming in with a paperback under his arm and a coffee he looks to be regretting, and Caleb’s mouth closes.
“Thirty,” Evan says, ticking off Jack’s name. “Thirty is when they stop calling it ABD and start calling it a lifestyle.” He moves on to Yusuf’s.

“At thirty I owned one coat and an opinion of Hume I have since had to retire,” Hale tells the table, taking the middle of the long side, where he can turn his head to either end. “Mr. Marsh has the better of me: he’s employed. We are done with Waugh. Mr. Costigan, the last page. I have a dean at half past two, and the man has not improved.”
Jack addresses the chair, currently Hale. “The lamp at the end’s a light somebody left on, Professor. Not an answer.”

Hale turns down the length of the table to the window end, out of a habit that is a week old, and says to the beige chair in the sun, “Miss Broussard, Mr. Costigan contends that the lamp is a light left on, not an answer —”
He stops.
“The chair,” Hale says, and hears it. “The chair is… addressing furniture.” He keeps his eyes on the empty seat until Caleb coughs. “Carry on.”
Jack has the rebuttal to the rebuttal built already, and it’s a good one, with a hinge in the middle of it, and there’s nowhere to take it. It sits in him, hot, till the hour is out.

At ten to two Hale holds up the paperback, a green Penguin gone soft at the spine. “There is no seminar Thursday next. The chair will be lecturing in Sacramento, to people paid to agree with it. Greene. *The End of the Affair.* For Monday the twenty-second, when the table will once again be in a position to contradict me.” He opens it and reads: “A story has no beginning or end: arbitrarily one chooses that moment of experience from which to look back or from which to look ahead.”
“The narrator tells you in a few pages that this is a record of hatred, more than of love,” he says, and shuts it. “He’s lying, the poor sod. Catch him at it.”
Caleb writes the first line down, colon and all. Jack doesn’t. He is going to buy the book.

By ten past eleven the Anchor is down to its night people: the harbor black in the windows, the pie case three-quarters gone, and on the end stool Merle with a bowl of chowder and a dollar’s worth of jukebox. The machine is playing the one Mariah Carey song it owns. No one has ever been caught choosing it. From the back booth, when it ends, comes a single “Brava,” and Merle looks up to see who’s being praised.

Hale has taken Evan to the back booth for his birthday. At the pass Gloria pins a ticket to the rail with the flat of her hand. “Two professors in my booth on a Thursday,” she says. “I’ll need a priest.”
“I can get you one,” Jack says. “He keeps Wednesday hours.”
“I need him tonight, hon. Wednesday’s no good to me.” She goes off with the pot.

Twenty minutes on, a plate comes back through the pass with a slice of olallieberry on it, cut by somebody with views on the angle. “From the booth,” Gloria says. “The one with the wine on his cuff. That’s my nine, hon. Eat it before the dishes find you.”

Jack eats it standing at the Hobart with the steam in his face, and through the pass he gets the booth in slices. Hale is on his third, house red in a juice glass, and is explaining something to Evan with both hands. Evan has coffee. When the third glass comes down Evan looks at it, and at the clock over the pie case, and back at his cup. Hale doesn’t see him do it.

At a quarter to one Hale pays at the register, and Jack, passing with a bus tub on his hip, hears his name. “Mr. Costigan.” Evan has already gone out to unlock his bike. Hale lays a twenty on a check about half that and doesn’t wait for change. “The table is very quiet, Mr. Costigan. I find I miss being contradicted.”
“I could contradict you now, Professor.”
“Not at this hour,” Hale says, getting an arm into his coat. “I’d only agree with you.” He goes out into the fog buttoned wrong by one.
Gloria wipes the counter down to the grain. “When’s she back?”
“The twenty-first. Sunday night.”

body: Yusuf is coming along the bluff path from the lot with a steel thermos, in the gray Marisol hoodie, at the pace of a man who has walked this path every morning for weeks. He walks at dawn now. He hasn’t said whose habit it is.
“It started last night,” Yusuf says, by way of hello, and takes the rail beside him with his eyes on the water. “Marjah. That’s when we heard. Over there it was already morning.”
Jack puts the pencil down on the clipboard. “Okay,” he says.

“Tariq’s been home since the twenty-third.” Yusuf unscrews the thermos. “He did the stairs, all fourteen, in January. Now he sits. My father bought a second television so they’d stop fighting over which channel, and now there are two, and they watch both.”
“Does he say anything?”

“They say it wrong. The anchors. Tariq corrects them, out loud, in a normal voice, to the screen, and then again in case they missed it. Dad turned the sound off the first night. Tariq turned it back on.” He pours tea into the thermos lid and watches it steam. “He knows the names of the roads.”
“My brother is home,” Yusuf says, “and he’s still over there.” He holds the lid out.
Jack takes it. It’s hot through the plastic.
“It’s tea,” Yusuf says. “Not coffee. I’m telling you now so there’s no face.”
It is black enough to read by and has cardamom in it. Jack drinks it down to the leaves. Yusuf reads the form over his shoulder.
“‘In New Mexico.’”
“It’s a location.”
“It’s a boundary condition,” Yusuf says, and holds out a hand for the stopwatch. “Give me that. I’ll call them. You write.”
They do ten. Yusuf calls the crests across the rock in the order they come, dry and unhurried, eleven, twelve, eleven, and Jack writes them down.
“Which column?” Yusuf asks, at the fourth.
“Hers,” Jack says, and writes it there in his own hand.

response: He opens it, and the little screen fills with a motel bathroom: a mirror still fogged at the corners from the shower, a fluorescent tube over it he can practically hear. Her, in the mirror. His flannel and nothing else. It hangs open down the middle, and her free hand holds it shut in one place, low, at her hip, and lets it go everywhere else. The tube light isn’t kind to anybody and she hasn’t asked it to be. The iPhone is up at her collarbone with its little apple shining back at the glass, and nobody but him is ever going to see this.

Her hair is dark. That’s the first thing and the strangest: Dell’s, it has to be, nearly black under the motel light, so that for the length of a breath it’s a stranger in a stranger’s bathroom — and then it’s her mouth, the corner of it coming up, and it’s Skye. A bath towel lies in a heap on the tile by her feet. On the mirror over her shoulder, in lipstick, there’s a lopsided heart and YOUNGSTOWN, the letters crowding up against each other at the end where she ran out of mirror.

He looks for as long as he looks. Over the footlocker the crucifix is on its nail in the lamplight, and he knows the word for what he is doing, and he does it anyway. Then he writes back the only thing there is in him.

s09b.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 15 · 12:01 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — HER VOICE FIRST
body: “Did you open it?”
“I wanted your voice first.”
On her end the motel heater knocks, and then it roars. “Open it now,” she says. “I’ll wait.”

So he does, with her on the line. He holds the RAZR up over his face at the end of his arm, her breathing coming small and tinny out of the earpiece, and the picture opens: the bathroom mirror fogged at the corners; his flannel and nothing else, hanging open, her hand holding it shut low at one hip and letting it go everywhere else; the tile, the towel; on the glass over her shoulder, in lipstick, a lopsided heart and YOUNGSTOWN. Her hair is dark. He doesn’t know her — a dark-haired girl in a motel, anybody — and then the corner of her mouth comes up and it’s Skye, so much Skye that he puts his free hand over his eyes.
She can’t see his face. She listens to it. “Well?”

“I didn’t know you,” he says. “Not at first. With the hair. And then it was your mouth.” He brings the phone back to his ear and has nothing to do with the other hand. “I want to be on that tile. I want it so much I can’t lie still on this bed.”
A long breath comes down the line, a laugh with the sound turned off.
Then she clears her throat and turns into a woman behind a front desk, all carpet and little brass bell and name tag: “This concludes our programming.”
He finds Theo’s desk clock across the dark room. “It’s Kevin’s birthday.”
“Tell Kevin happy birthday from the flannel.”
“I’m not telling him that.”
“Tell him from Dell.” And then, close to the phone, with the voice gone out of it: “Goodnight, Jack.”
She’s gone before he says it back.

The handkerchief is a real one, ironed. Theo’s hand comes down on the gray shoulder and stays there while the man weeps at the same curb, over the same Navigator, apparently for the same reason.
Four of them out of the car, not five.

Kevin is first through the doors, the tag still on his roller bag in his mother’s marker, CALL MA WHEN YOU LAND, and under it now in his own, *DONE. —K.* Jack holds up the plate. Kevin reads the foil, then Jack, then the Bic that comes out of the Carhartt, and says, “I’m not going to ask why you carry that. Clinically, I’m worried.”
“Open flame in a common area is a violation,” Priya says from the desk, and then, reading Kevin’s face, “Five seconds.” She clicks the stopwatch.
Kevin shuts his eyes scrubbing-in tight and blows it out in three.

The remaining ten concern Kevin’s grandmother, who outranks the archbishop.” She takes the fork out of Kevin’s hand and eats a bite of his birthday. “Quality control.”

Laney comes through the lobby at a quarter to ten at night in sunglasses, with four bags and a garment bag over her shoulder like a body she’s disposing of. “Kevin, happy birthday, sugar,” she says, and kisses the air a foot from his cheek, and goes past Jack to the elevator as if he were the Pepsi machine.
“She did that to a Cinnabon in Dallas,” Kevin says, and looks at the crust. “I mean it as comfort. It doesn’t comfort me either.” He smiles, and it is a perfectly good smile, and he finishes it.

By ten past ten Theo has hung ten coats in the closet of 412 in the order he packed them, shoulder to shoulder, and still has the camel on, a minute longer than a coat needs to stay on a man in a heated room. He takes it off at last and hangs it last.

Then he turns with something purple and gold in his hand. “Brees threw them,” he says. “Possibly someone near Brees.” A strand of Bacchus beads, plastic, the green gone fogged where a thumb has been holding it. He doesn’t hand it over. He crosses to the nail over Jack’s footlocker where the crucifix hangs and loops the strand so it falls to either side of the corpus like a stole, steps back, looks at what he’s done, and leaves it.
“I held your seat,” he tells the closet.
“I told you not to.”
“You did. The coat had a lovely time.”
“How was it?”
“It was a parade, Costigan.” He sits on his bed and lines his shoes up, toes to the wall. “It went by.”

Jack has had Theo’s weekends since September in three acts and a credit sequence, with floor plans. This is the review. On the bedspread the iPhone lights up face-up, and lights up again, and goes dark. Theo doesn’t turn it over.
“Tell me about the films,” he says.
So Jack does, film by film. Theo takes every answer to the end, with a sock in his hand, and asks one question at a time and doesn’t once say *Picture it*.
“And the sheriff’s daughter?”
“Snow. She says Sunday.”
“I’m glad,” Theo says, and it is short.

He turns the lamp off himself. Through the blind the streetlight reaches the nail and finds the beads, purple, gold, a fogged green, hanging to either side of the cross. Wednesday the Church goes purple. The nail is early.

Tuesday is Fat Tuesday, and Youngstown observes it in lard. A white bakery box fills in from the top down, powdered sugar last: open on the Costigans’ kitchen table, the sugar on the oilcloth, a jelly bleeding through the paper.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. body: The picture came while he slept, and by the time he’s climbing Ocean Road toward the noon Mass he has opened it so often that the RAZR has stopped dimming the screen to save him. A forehead, blurred where she moved: a thumbprint cross in gray, dark hair swept back off it, a motel doorframe behind with its paint coming off in strips.

body.text: they gave me one. am i allowed. the makeup girl crossed herself and wiped it off for continuity
youre allowed

body: He sent that over the oatmeal. It’s all he’ll eat until dark.

By five past twelve St. Brendan’s has a line out the doors and down the courtyard. No other weekday can do it: six men from Sigma Rho in a pack with their letters on, the women’s soccer team in warm-ups with their cleats looped around their necks, and the once-a-year people along the back wall, standing as if they might be asked to leave. Peter Haddad works the door with worship aids and no hope of enough. Gus has the organ going under all of them.

Osei preaches a short one on a Gospel that tells everyone to anoint their heads and wash their faces so no one will know they’re fasting, and then sends them up the aisle to be marked in front of God and Sigma Rho. “Yes,” he says, to the objection before anyone has made it. “I see it too. The ash is only the label on the bottle, my friends. Take the medicine.”

The line goes up the center aisle in two files, and the choir takes it over their heads, *Parce, Domine, parce populo tuo*, spare, Lord, spare your people, slow, as Gus likes it, so the line can’t hurry. Jack picks Osei’s file. Ahead of him a Sigma Rho sophomore takes the thumb and answers *Amen* loud enough that the soccer team turns around.

Then it’s Jack. The thumb comes up gray out of the little bowl and smells of a cold fireplace, and Osei says it as he says it to everyone: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” The thumb goes down and across, grit on the skin. Osei’s eyes stay on his for the length of the sentence. Not a word more from either side of the thumb. Then the next forehead.
Becca steps up as he turns, in her buttoned coat, and says it to the side of his face, low, in the church voice, entirely sincere: “Yours is very even.”
“Thank you, Becca. Yours will be too.”
She nods at that and goes up to the thumb.

body.text: At Communion he goes up with the line, ashes and all. It’s the second time this week, and it still surprises his knees.
body.else: At Communion he stays in the pew with the ash on his forehead, and the line goes up past his knees, half of it frat boys who have no idea he’s anybody.

body: Kevin catches him at the courtyard gate with a thumb-sized smudge, a calculator in a plastic sleeve and a pencil behind each ear. “Orgo at two,” he says. “My blood sugar is a cliff and the exam is at the bottom of it.”
“You get two small meals. The Church says.”
“Two collations that don’t add up to a full meal. I’m saving mine for the third hour of the exam. It’s called pacing.” He heads for the science quad at a walk that wants to be a run.

body.text: Leaving, over his shoulder: “Still no answer to what I wanted instead. I’m giving up guessing for Lent.”
body.else: Leaving, over his shoulder: “Pray for my orgo. It’s a corporal work of mercy. Visiting the sick.”

body: By four the ash on the Delgado steps has gone to class and come back: every third forehead, a lot of them faint, and a girl in a bathrobe being told by a boy in a Packers hat that she’s allowed to wash it. Jack, on the third step, hasn’t.
The RAZR’s outside screen shows its row of dashes. Wednesday. The recording runs its length, *an inmate at an Ohio correctional institution*, Danny’s name jammed into the gap, and he presses one.
“Professor.” The dayroom behind him is louder than last time; somebody has a judge show on. “Ma blabbed already, I know. Got her letter.”

body.text: “She said she would. *Small. Make him work for it.*”
body.else: “She said she’d write you from New Mexico.”

body: “She meant it.” Paper moves near the mouthpiece. “She wrote small, Professor. Like ants. Except the capitals. Top of the first page, you ready, in capitals: THE GOAT AT CARRILLO.”

body.text: “I had Carrillo from the source. Now I got an eyewitness. You’re worse in capitals.”
body.else: “What’s Carrillo? Don’t tell me. She told me. In capitals.”

body: “She sent a picture of a horse. Sorrel. Name of Clementine. It’s on my wall where Reggie has to look at it. Reggie says it looks at him.”
“What did you say?”
“I said that’s the point of a horse. And the chaplain came down the range at noon with a thumb. Seventeen guys on the tier. Reggie asked for seconds.”
“You can’t get seconds.”
“That’s what the chaplain said. Reggie says in Portsmouth you ask till somebody says no twice.” The television roars at something and falls back. “You get yours?”
“Noon Mass. It’s still on.”
A chair scrapes. When Danny comes back he has dropped his voice for the thing he called to ask. “You going up Sunday?”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’ Ash Wednesday, collect: Skye’s letter came. She wrote small, like ants, except the capitals. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO. The horse is on his wall where Reggie has to look at it. The chaplain came down the range with ashes and Reggie asked for seconds. Then he asked was I going up Sunday. I told him I don’t go up. He didn’t ask why. Least you’re going, he said. Don’t stop going. That’s the whole trouble with him.

response: “I stay in the pew, Dan. I go. I just don’t go up.”
Danny doesn’t ask why. “Huh.” On the line the dayroom goes on without either of them: the television, a chair, a man calling a number down the tier.
“Least you’re going,” Danny says. Then: “Don’t stop going, Professor. That’s the whole trouble with *me*.”

He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’ Ash Wednesday, collect: Skye’s letter came. She wrote small, like ants, except the capitals. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO. The horse is on his wall where Reggie has to look at it. The chaplain came down the range with ashes and Reggie asked for seconds. Then he asked was I going up Sunday. I asked him to pray for me. He does already. It’s in the schedule: count, chow, me.

response: “I do that already. It’s in the schedule. Count, chow, you.” Somebody behind him yells for the phone. “You want me to do it louder?”
“Medium.”
“Medium, I can do.”

choices.text: “I go up for the donuts after.”
choices.key: On Ash Wednesday you told Danny you go up for the donuts.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’ Ash Wednesday, collect: Skye’s letter came. She wrote small, like ants, except the capitals. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO. The horse is on his wall where Reggie has to look at it. The chaplain came down the range with ashes and Reggie asked for seconds. Then he asked was I going up Sunday. I told him I go up for the donuts. He let me have it. Then he didn’t say anything for a while.

response: Danny laughs, once, and lets him have it, and the quiet afterward is a long way from believing him. “Okay, Professor.”
*You have one minute remaining,* the recording says.

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 17 · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE LIGHT, AND LENT
body: The courtyard still smells of noon: burned palm, wax on the flagstones where somebody’s taper dripped, a hundred people’s coats. Out past the bluff a crescent moon so thin it’s barely a mark is going down into the sea to the west. Jack hasn’t washed his forehead. He hasn’t eaten since a bowl of oatmeal at seven, either, and his stomach has been audible since four.

The bulb is on. The tape on the kneeler has held a week. He kneels on it with the ash still on him and the day’s hunger making him light in the head, and the closet is the closet: old wool, the radiator, whoever came before him.

body.text: He kneels and tells the linen he has nothing new since last week. It’s the truth. He has kept his word seven days, and he says so flatly, like Mass times off a bulletin, because there’s nothing in it to be proud of: seven days, with the room at the bottom of the hill dark and the girl it belongs to in New Mexico. The beads click on the far side. “A week is a long time,” Osei says. “Longer than it sounds.”
body.else: He kneels and tells the linen he has nothing new since last week — and nothing different, either. The same thing. And he still can’t say the other. Osei doesn’t make him say it twice. “I heard it last week. I believe you.” The shadow of the hand on the linen, the blessing again, Father and Son and Spirit. “That is what Wednesdays are for. Not only that. Also that.”

body: He gives the linen one more thing, because it’s been in his pocket all day with the pack. “Skye got ashes this morning. In Santa Fe, before work. She sent me a picture and asked was she allowed.”
“And what did you tell her?”
“That she was.”

“You told her right. Dust is the one thing in this Church nobody has to qualify for.” The chair creaks. “It is Lent,” Osei says, in case the news hasn’t reached Jack’s forehead. “Tonight people will give up a great many things. Chocolate. Beer. Swearing, which never lasts past the first parking lot. Do not give up the Wednesdays for Lent. People try. It never works the way they mean it to.” He shifts on the far side. “Forty days. I have done it every year of my life that I can remember. You will find I am not good at it either. The prophet says to tear your heart and leave your coat alone. I have always liked that. A coat is expensive.”
So Jack tells the linen his, aloud. Said on the kneeler it’s a different animal than it was on the walk down. No cigarettes. And every Friday a fast, like today, all forty days.
“Why those?”
“Because they’re the ones I’ll notice.”
“Ɛyɛ,” Osei says. “Small and hard. Those are the ones that work.”

body.text: The soft pack is in the Carhartt’s left pocket while he says it, nineteen in it, one gone since the loading dock the day of the card.
body.else: The soft pack is in the Carhartt’s left pocket while he says it, the cellophane still on it.

body: Out the side door afterward the courtyard is empty, and the olive tree leans over the wall with the streetlight caught in its leaves. He stands under it with his hand in the left pocket, closed around the pack.

choices.key: For Lent you gave up cigarettes and kept the pack in your pocket, shut.
response: He keeps it. He takes his hand out and zips the pocket shut over the pack, and the corners of it press through the lining against his hip, a small square weight he’ll have for forty days. His hands already want something to do. He puts them in his other pockets, on purpose, and they go on wanting.

choices.text: *Give it to Father Osei to keep.*
choices.key: For Lent you gave up cigarettes and gave Father Osei the pack to keep.
response: The side door opens behind him: Osei, in the cassock, with the ring of keys, come out to lock up. He sees Jack under the tree and stops. Jack holds the pack out to him across the flagstones.

Osei takes it without looking at it and puts it in his cassock pocket like a bulletin somebody handed him at the door. “If you need it,” he says, “you will have to come up the hill and ask me for it. In person.” He locks the side door and tries the handle. “I will want a reason.”

choices.text: *Bury it in the sand can on the loading dock on the way home.*
choices.key: For Lent you gave up cigarettes and buried the pack in the sand can on the loading dock.
response: Delgado’s loading dock at nine: the dumpsters, the tower of milk crates, the Folgers can of sand by the kitchen door with the butts standing up in it. He pushes the pack down into the sand with his thumb until it’s gone and smooths the top over it.

It’s the cleanest break there is. It’s also five dollars and change at the 7-Eleven at the bottom of the hill, and he knows it, because he’s from Youngstown, and in Youngstown everybody knows what everything costs.

s13.slug: THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 18 · 4:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE STAIRS → 1:25 AM · 412 — LENA BACK
body: The sun has got low enough by half past four to come in under the lobby’s overhang and lie across the tile in a long yellow slant, with the shadow of the bike rack printed on it like a fence. Jack has his Anchor apron rolled up in one fist and his mail in the other: a letter from Ma with a coupon folded inside it for a Giant Eagle two thousand miles away, and a quarter sheet from Newman announcing Stations of the Cross, Fridays at 7:00 PM, in Becca’s handwriting with a little cross drawn over the *i* in *Fridays*. Down the wall of little brass doors, 217’s is where it always is, in the shade at the far end. He keeps his eyes on his own and his key in it.
Doug comes off the elevator in socks and a Tauren druid T-shirt with a party-size bag of Funyuns, sees him, and changes course.

“Dude.” He falls in beside Jack at the foot of the stairs. “Dude. Did you hear? Lena and the guitar guy. *Done.* Pete from his band told Priya’s friend’s roommate — it was, like, Valentine’s, by *text*, which is cold, dude, and now he’s playing all minor chords at the Bastille, like, on purpose —”
Jack keeps walking. Doug stays at the bottom with the Funyuns, still going — “which, musically, dude, is a *choice* —” — and the stairwell takes the rest and hands back only the echo.

From the third-floor landing the window gives him the curb. A black car with the trunk up. Laney comes down the front steps at a run, in socks, and stops a yard short of it like there’s a line painted on the concrete. Lena gets out of the back with a duffel on her shoulder and no pie box. When Laney gets her arms around her, Laney’s face is over Lena’s shoulder, toward the building: eyes shut tight, mouth pressed flat, the sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Jack is up the next flight before they’re through the doors.

At the Anchor he is very fast. Racks go into the Hobart and come out in a roll of steam and go up on the shelf still dripping; the stockpots are done by ten and the mats hosed by midnight, and at eleven Rudy says so from the flattop, like a complaint. “Slow down. There’s nothing left to wash.”

When he gets in, 412 is dark except for the streetlight. It comes through the blind and lays its bars up the wall and finds Theo’s beads on the nail. Jack doesn’t hit the light. He comes in with the Hobart still on him — lemon sanitizer, hot rinse, the bottom of somebody’s clam chowder — and sits on the edge of his bed to get his shoes off. Across the room the closet door stands open on ten coats hung shoulder to shoulder in the dark, like a congregation that came early.
Theo is on his back with his hands folded on his chest, and his eyes are open. The streetlight is in them.
“She ended it with Julian. In New Orleans, last week. Her decision — nobody’s idea but hers.”
Jack gets the left shoe off and sets it by the footlocker, toe to the wall.

It’s information. He starts on the right shoe. There’s a knot in the lace from the Anchor, wet and pulled tight, and he works at it with his thumbnail, and works at it, and then just pulls, and the lace snaps off in his hand down by the eyelet.

He sits there in the stripes holding the end of it, and for no reason he wants he thinks of Julian beside her in the pew at the nine o’clock in November, with his hands folded, saying the responses half a line behind everybody else, learning them by ear, and never going up.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s.
