Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Thursday there was a card in my box, cream, her mother’s, in her hand. Theo says I’m not coming. Her mother’s made up the twins’ room. American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat. I’d be welcome. At Hale’s we didn’t say a word to each other; everything went through the chair. After, I slid the card back down the table. She stopped it with two fingers before it went off the edge and put it in her bag. Thursday, February eighteenth, from the stairwell window: a car at the curb, Laney down the steps at a run, Lena out of the back with a duffel. Doug says she and the guitar guy are done. That night Theo told me in the dark: she ended it with Julian, in New Orleans, last week. Her decision. Nobody’s idea but hers.

choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you said okay.
response: A car goes by in the street below and drags the stripes off the ceiling and puts them back.
“Okay,” Theo says from his bed, in the same voice, as if the two of them have agreed on something.

choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you asked him why he was telling you.
response: “Pruitt’s been telling the elevator since four. So you’d hear it from somebody who wasn’t him.”
Theo, who can talk for ten minutes about a lens, leaves it there. No pitch in it, no camera. It’s true, and he doesn’t dress it.

choices.text: “Tell Julian nothing. Send the flowers yourself, on the good stock.”
choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you told him to send the flowers himself, on the good stock.
response: Theo says nothing. The beads on the nail catch the light from a car and let it go.
“I’m going to pretend I was asleep for that, Costigan.” The bedsprings go as he rolls toward the window, and that is the last of Theo for the night.

s13a.slug: FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 19 · 1:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOADING DOCK — LENT, DAY THREE

body.text: From the other bed, after a while, while Jack is finding his shoes in the dark: “I’m not going to ask you which one.” And he doesn’t.
body.else: Theo’s breathing goes long and even in the other bed, asleep or giving a good impression of it, while Jack finds his shoes in the dark.

body: He takes the Carhartt off its hook by feel and goes down the back stairs with the shoes in his hand, the right one with its lace knotted together where it broke, and puts them on at the bottom on the cold concrete.

The dock at this hour belongs to the sodium lamp over the kitchen door. Everything under it is the same orange: the dumpsters, the tower of milk crates, the bike racks with one stripped Huffy chained to them since September. Past the lot the eucalyptus is going in the wind off the lagoon, menthol and cat and rain that hasn’t come yet. The only other light on this side of the building is a window up on three with a Saints flag thumbtacked across it, hung on the seventh by somebody from Metairie and never taken down.

It comes up the back of his throat first, a Marlboro he hasn’t had: the paper, the first hot pull, as exact as the smell of a kitchen in another state. His hands find out after. They want the small business of it, the tap and the shake and the match cupped against the wind, and they have had nothing to do since Wednesday.

body.text: The pack is in the Carhartt where he put it Wednesday night, zipped in, and through the lining his fingers have found its corners and the soft give of the foil top on their own.

He has no pack. Osei has it, in a cassock pocket, up a hill, and would want a reason. At the bottom of the other hill the 7-Eleven sign is lit all night, red and green and orange, and from the end of the dock he can see the top of it over the roof of the parking structure.
The Folgers can is right there by his shoe, where it always is, and his pack is in it, under an inch of sand and somebody else’s butts.

body: In the right-hand pocket, against his hip, the tin.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Lent: no cigarettes. Two in the morning after the first Thursday of it, on the dock, I opened the tin and counted. Eleven.

response: The tin comes out warm from the pocket. The hinge gives with its small dry complaint, and under the orange light the cigarettes lie in their row.

He counts them with the tip of his little finger, one to eleven, and then back down from eleven to one, because a count that only goes one direction isn’t finished. Eleven. He shuts the lid and keeps the tin in his fist until his fist is warm again, and puts it back in the right-hand pocket.

He leaves his hands where they are, one on the corners of the pack and one on the tin, and stands under the lamp till they stop asking. It takes the eucalyptus going quiet and starting up again, twice.

One out of the soft pack, and a match from an Anchor book, cupped. The first drag goes down like a word he promised on a kneeler not to say. Lent, day three. He smokes it to the filter at the edge of the dock with the orange light on his hands, and doesn’t enjoy any of it except all of it.
He sits down on the edge of the dock with his feet hanging over the ramp and his hands under his thighs, and he stays there till the 7-Eleven is just a sign again.

Down the hill with his hands in his pockets. Five dollars and change, and a clerk eating sunflower seeds out of the bag who rings it up without lifting his eyes from a crossword. One, on the curb outside by the ice machine. The other nineteen go in the trash can beside it, which is the stupidest thing he has ever paid for.
He sets the side of his shoe against the can and keeps it there, a little pressure, until he is cold enough to go back upstairs.

Two fingers in the sand. The pack comes up gritty and a little damp, and he lights one with sand still on the filter, and it tastes of the can, and he smokes it anyway, standing over the hole he made, down to nothing.

s14.slug: FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 19 · 6:40 PM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE FIRST FRIDAY
body: On the first Friday of Lent, Anacapa Commons does the fish. It comes as a breaded square, perfectly square, of something white that was never that shape in the ocean, with a lemon wedge and a paper cup of tartar sauce, and Jack eats every bit of it at a table by the window because it’s the meal. One today, and this is it. He’s hungry in a clean, specific way, and he mentions it to nobody. In Youngstown the baccalà has been soaking in Nonna’s enamel basin on the cellar stairs since Tuesday, the water changed three times a day like she’s nursing it, and tonight it’s on the table on Glenwood with the potatoes and the good oil, and none of it is here.
Kevin’s text was waiting when he sat down.

body.text: Fasting, and the orgo curve came out. I’ve become a monk with a calculator.

body: His tray is on the conveyor when the RAZR goes again. It’s her. He takes it outside.

The Commons steps are emptying into the dusk. The light has gone down behind the Delgado roofline and left the sky over it lit from underneath, and on her end there’s a bar in Santa Fe: glasses, a jukebox nobody is listening to, somebody’s boot heels coming down off a table, and a crew of grown men singing something with a great deal of whistling in it.
“It’s a wrap party,” Skye says, over it. “I’m wrapped. Dell’s wrapped. The horse is wrapped and doesn’t know it yet.”

She tells him the rest with her mouth close to the phone. Corinne’s office has her on a plane into Burbank Sunday at noon, a car, a meeting Monday about the next thing. And this afternoon, in the motel parking lot, on her own phone, Skye rebooked herself onto Saturday’s last flight into Santa Barbara, through Phoenix, and nobody’s office knows yet. Her mother, next door, is going to find out from a note on the connecting-door pillow.
“Corinne’s going to find out from the *airline*,” she says, and somebody behind her whoops at something else entirely.
Jack is on his feet on the Commons steps. He doesn’t remember standing up.
“9:52,” she says. “Don’t stall it at the curb.”
“I won’t.”
“You will. Do it after I’m in the car.” The whistling swells up behind her, and somebody yells *Skye!* across the bar like a toast, and she says she has to go be thrown in the air.
He has the Saab and he has Saturday. He doesn’t sleep much.

s15.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20 · 9:52 PM · SANTA BARBARA AIRPORT — THE CURB
body: He washes the sweatshirt in the morning, as instructed. Machine three, warm, a capful of Doug’s detergent because his own ran out Thursday, and then the dryer at the end of the row with the round glass door, where he stands with his arms folded and watches the gray CREW go by, and by, and by, like the one fish in a dentist’s tank. Doug comes in behind him with a laundry basket holding nothing but World of Warcraft T-shirts and stops in the door.
“Dude.” All five vowels. “Are you *crying* at a dryer?”
“It’s the sheets.”
Doug looks at the dryer. There is one sweatshirt in it. “What sheets?”

At two he takes the Saab through the car wash on Hollister, the one with the big blue brushes that come down on the windshield like a pair of golden retrievers who have missed him, and it stalls at the exit under the blowers, and the kid with the chamois knocks on his window to ask if he’s okay.

The airport is the old one, from the war: white stucco, red tile, arched windows, palms lit from underneath, a terminal about the size of the parish hall at St. Brigid’s. There is one arrivals curb and one airport cop to keep it, a heavyset man with a whistle on a lanyard who has already waved the Saab on twice. Jack has done two loops of the lot road. On the third the radio is playing a song about airplanes that he doesn’t know, which seems like a lot to ask of a coincidence, and he leaves it on low and puts the hazards on and sits at the curb as small as a Saab can sit.

The hat rides shotgun. It has been on the shelf over his own bed in 412 for two weeks, crown down, beside the Fenner textbook; he took it off her closet shelf the morning she left, with the key, and couldn’t have told anybody why, and nobody asked. Tonight it came down the hill on the passenger seat. It’s the only way a Stetson should travel.

At 9:49 a plane comes in low over the slough with its landing lights on, and he watches it down behind the terminal roof and has no way of knowing whether it’s hers. 9:52. The sliding doors open and let out a man with golf clubs and a family of five with a car seat between them, and close, and open again.

body.text: A girl comes out in a sheepskin coat, with a carry-on and a suitcase, and his eyes go right past her. Dark hair to her shoulders, nearly black under the terminal lights: somebody’s daughter, home from somewhere, nobody he’s met. He saw a strip of that hair once, above a thumbprint of ash on a screen the size of a stamp, and it didn’t get him ready for any of this. Then the girl sees the Saab, and her chin comes up, and her mouth starts going at one corner before the rest of her has decided to, and it’s her.
body.else: She comes out in the sheepskin coat with the carry-on and the suitcase, and he’s seen the hair already, dark against a motel mirror on a screen two inches tall. Under the terminal lights it’s a different thing, darker and real, and the face under it is the one he knows best in the world, so that the hair looks like part of the costume, something she has on and hasn’t gotten around to taking off.

body: The bank sign across the road says fifty-eight degrees, and she has the sheepskin collar turned up around her ears. Under the coat, buttoned to the throat, is his flannel.

She comes straight to the open passenger window and leans in to say something to him, and finds the hat. She laughs, one short surprised sound. Then she reaches in with both hands and takes it off the seat and puts it on, there at the curb under the sodium lights in front of the cop and the golf clubs and God: the brownie-pan Stetson her mother said she would not wear in an airport. She tips it back off her forehead with one finger.
Jack is out of the car on the street side with the door hanging open and the radio still going, grinning at her across the Saab’s roof.

response: He comes around the hood. She lets go of the suitcase on the way to meet him and it tips over on the curb behind her with a slap, and it can stay there. She hits him at a run with both arms around his neck, and he takes her up off the curb, coat and all, the weight of the sheepskin, her boots off the ground, and the hat goes somewhere over his shoulder into the loading zone. She smells like the inside of an airplane and motel soap, and under that, her.
“I’m not in the airport.” She points down at her boots, at the painted edge of the curb under the toes of them. “I’m at the *curb*.”
And then she comes around the back of the Saab at him, hat and all, and the brim gets him in the forehead before the rest of her does.

“I came home *on time*.” She’s around the back of the Saab and into him, up on the toes of her boots, and then up on the toes of his, standing on his feet like a kid at a wedding. She says the rest into his collar. “They had me late.”

s15a.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20 · 9:58 PM · SBA ARRIVALS → HOLLISTER → THE 217
body: They kiss at the curb with the hazards going. It’s two weeks long and it keeps going: her cold hands up under his jaw, his inside the sheepskin at her back where the shirt is still warm from the plane, her mouth opening under his, her whole weight coming onto him, the brim of the hat bent against his ear, until a whistle goes off three feet away.
The cop has one hand on his belt and the whistle still in his teeth. He takes it out. “Ma’am. Sir.” He nods at the blinking Saab. “It’s a *loading* zone.”
Skye doesn’t let go of Jack’s collar. “We’re loading.”

body.text: Under the brim, for him only: “Go on. Say it.” “*Mm.*” “Called it.”

body: The suitcase goes in the back seat with the carry-on on top of it; the hat goes on the dash, crown down, rocking. Jack gets behind the wheel with the cop watching from the curb, puts in the clutch, finds first, lets it out as he has let it out fifty times in two weeks — and the Saab bucks once and dies, under the light, in front of the cop, who doesn’t move a muscle of his face about it.
Skye is already laughing. “Move over, Youngstown.”

They trade places around the hood — probably a second violation — and she drives. She drives the Saab like a limb she’d forgotten she had: second gear before the end of the curb, the clutch going in and out under her boot without a sound, the car taking it from her without a word of complaint.
Under the airport road’s lights, with her window down and the night coming in off the slough, her hair goes almost blue. She catches him looking at it.
“Twelve washes,” she says. “Corinne’s counting.” She pushes it back off her forehead with her wrist. “She refers to it as the situation.”

body.text: At the light by the long-term lot she keeps her eyes on the signal. “Did you open it?”
“Not yet.”
“Don’t.” The light changes, and she shifts up. “I want to be there when you do.”

body: At the red light on Hollister she puts the Saab in neutral and turns her head and looks at him, and her look has gone old, an old man’s, heavy-lidded, a look that has been up since yesterday and has stood in a lot of kitchen doorways after midnight, and her voice comes from somewhere down at the bottom of the coat, slow and tired, no question mark on anything.
“*Where were you.*”
“Here,” Jack says.

She holds the old man’s eyes on him the length of the red, and then they’re gone and it’s her, in the dashboard light, biting the inside of her cheek. The light goes green. Somebody behind them leans on his horn. She lets him.

On the 217 her right hand comes off the gearshift and lands on his thigh and stays, and when she has to shift she does it with her left hand reaching all the way across her own body, twice, badly, and still doesn’t take the right one back. The road is two miles long. The marsh opens up dark on one side and the campus lights come up ahead, and her hand is warm through his jeans the length of it, her thumb moving now and then and going nowhere. He sits in the passenger seat of her car with the salt coming in the window and the hat rocking on the dash and her hand on him.

s16.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20 · 10:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE LONG NIGHT IN
body: It has taken them thirty-five minutes to do twelve minutes of road, and the gravel turnout by the slough accounts for most of it. Sol’s house is dark. Sol is in Ojai again, Skye says, and Tomás is down on the boat for the weekend; the porch light is off, and the porch leans a little toward the street, as it always has. Off the bluff the surf is up tonight, a long slow set coming in out of the dark and going over against the foot of the stairs.

She can’t find the key. She goes through the coat on the top step, every pocket, both sides, laughing at herself, and hands him what she finds as she finds it: a boarding pass, a motel key card with a cartoon roadrunner on it, a call sheet folded into a square, a lip balm, a guitar pick that isn’t hers, two flat foil packets of Pop-Tarts. His hands are full by the time the keys turn up in the last pocket she tries, the inside one, over her heart.

body.text: Ten days ago, on a strip of gaffer tape, he said *I mean to stop*. The key is warm from her hand. He takes the ring from her, finds the right one by feel in the dark, and opens the door himself.

body: Inside, the front room smells of Sol’s plants, wet soil and the green pepper smell of the big fig by the window, and of the house, old wood and salt. She takes the boarding pass and the Pop-Tarts and the rest out of his hands in one armful and dumps it on the hall table, and crosses the dark room without touching anything, and on her way past the turntable on its milk crate by the window she lifts the arm and sets the needle down with one hand, not stopping.
“Sol leaves a record on for the plants,” she says.
The needle finds its groove with a hiss, and a bass line comes up into the dark, unhurried, and a woman’s voice somewhere behind it, low, somebody with all night to say it in.

She comes back across the room and stops a step short of him, close enough that he can smell the plane on her, and motel soap, and somebody else’s shampoo in the dark hair, something with coconut that isn’t hers. He puts his hands in it. It’s her hair with the shine gone out of it, dry at the ends where the color took, and when he pushes it back off her face with both hands her cheekbones are cold from the car window, and she’s warm everywhere his hands go after that.

They get as far as the bottom of the stairs. She hangs the hat on the newel post herself, a girl hanging her hat in a saloon, and she’s still in the coat when he has her against the banister with his mouth on her throat above the collar of the shirt. Her hands are already under his sweatshirt at the small of his back, cold as the porch rail, so that he says something about it into her neck, and she laughs and spreads her fingers wider on purpose.

Two weeks ago he was learning her. He isn’t learning anymore. His hands go where they mean to go, in under the coat and the shirt to the warm skin over her ribs, his thumb along the underside of her breast, and her breath catches exactly where he wanted it to, and he’s the one who turns her on the bottom stair so she’s a step above him and they’re eye to eye, and the one who starts on the buttons from the top. She lets him. She likes it, and tells him so against his ear, in a voice he has never heard on her. “Look at you.”

Two buttons down, she’s gone. She takes his wrist and stops it there, and looks at him from one step up with Dell Harlan’s eyes — flat, patient, done with him already, a girl who has spent her life waiting in kitchens for men to get to the point — and says, short and quick and bored, “Think about how long you’ve been standing on that stair.”

It goes straight down the back of his neck. He doesn’t play the sheriff. He doesn’t play anything. He picks her up off the step — she is lighter than the coat — and carries her up, and by the landing she’s laughing too hard to be anybody but herself, the flat eyes gone, her arms locked around his neck and her heels knocking the wall on every stair, saying his name with the laugh still in it. That’s the one he missed.

On the landing her boots go, one and then the other, kicked down the stairs, the second one going to the bottom a stair at a time like somebody leaving in a hurry. His sweatshirt goes over the rail. She gets out of her jeans against the wall with his help, hopping, swearing at the button in a whisper, and the shirt is open all the way down under the coat now, and there’s nothing under it. She tells him what she wants, straight out, with her mouth on his. He tells her the same.

They make it as far as her doorway. The mattress is right there across the room on the floor, the blanket on it, the lamp beside it on the boards, the string of Christmas bulbs dark over the window — four steps away, and it might as well be in New Mexico.

response: Her hands go to the collar to shrug out of it, and he catches the lapels instead, a fistful of sheepskin in each hand, and takes her down with him onto the floorboards of her own doorway. The coat comes down under her and opens around her like a pelt laid out by a fire. Wool and cold air and jet fuel come up out of it, and the motel, and her.

He puts his mouth on her in the middle of all that fleece, the notch of her throat, her breastbone, her breast, and she arches up off the wool into it. His hand goes down the length of her and she lifts herself into it, saying his name, one bare heel braced against the doorframe.

She gets his belt. She’s faster at it than he is and proud of it, and she looks up at him from the coat, the dark hair spilled out over the white wool where it doesn’t belong. “Now,” she says. “Here.”

He doesn’t argue. He gets an arm under her inside the coat and pulls her up to him, and it takes the breath out of both of them, and she grabs the coat’s collar on either side of her head and hangs on to it like a rope.

It’s fast. It has no patience in it at all. Two weeks are in it, the snow and the phone and the plane, and the boards knock against the threshold, and her heels are at the backs of his thighs, pulling. The coat slides. They go with it, a foot across the floor into the room, and don’t stop for it. She lets go of the collar and drags his mouth down onto hers, and she comes like that, all at once, a sound going out of her and into him, the empty sleeves of the coat flung out on either side of her. He goes over a moment after with her name in his mouth against hers, and keeps moving through it until there’s nothing left in him to move with.
Downstairs, a long way off, something soft lets go of the newel post and drops to the floor of the hall.

They lie in the doorway on the coat with the record still going below them. Her hair is stuck to his cheek. One bare foot is out on the cold boards past the hem, and the rest of her is under him in the wool, the shirt twisted half off one shoulder, her heart slamming against his chest.
“That was the hat,” she says.
“That was the hat.”
She looks past his shoulder at the mattress, four steps away with its blanket on it. “I own a *bed*,” she says. “I *own* one.”

choices.text: *Turn the lamp on. You want to see her.*
response: The lamp is on the floor by the mattress, where it lives. He lets go of her long enough to cross to it on his knees and turn it on.

When he looks back she’s where he left her, on the floorboards in the doorway, up on her elbows in the open coat, blinking at the light and then at him. It’s a forty-watt bulb in a paper shade from Target and it turns the room small and gold. He comes back to her on his knees, and she watches him cross back to her, and her lips part a little and stay that way.
He gets the coat off her shoulders and down her arms, and the shirt after it, and spreads them both under her on the boards, and she lies back on them in the light.

He looks at her. He doesn’t hurry it. The flush already starting up her chest; a bruise the size of a plum on her shin from a horse trailer in New Mexico that he’s seeing for the first time; the freckle on her hip he could find blind; the dark rinse fanned out over his own flannel, and her face under it, looking right back at him. She lies in the gold and lets him look, and her breathing changes while he does it.

He kisses her from the mouth down, slow at first, and can’t keep it slow, and her hips come up off the boards to meet his hand, and he watches her face the entire time: the line that comes between her eyebrows, her lip caught in her teeth and let go, her eyes going unfocused and coming back to find him. He has never watched anybody this close. He has never been let.
“Come here,” she says, and pulls him up by the hair. “I want to see you too.”

She gets his jeans down with her heels. They come together with the lamp on them both, urgent and fast, the boards hard under his knees and her hands hard on his back, and he can see everything — the red his jaw has left on her throat, the sweat at her hairline under the dark, the moment her mouth opens and nothing comes out of it. She keeps her eyes on him. When it takes her he watches it go through her face in the light, the thing he wanted, and it takes him along with it, her name breaking in half in his mouth.
After, they’re a heap in the doorway, half on the coat and half on the bare floor, the shirt rucked up under her shoulder blades.
She turns her head on the boards toward the lamp, and back. “You turned on a *light*,” she says, “to do it on the *floor*.”
“I wanted to see you.”
“You saw me.” She says it quietly, and it isn’t a joke, and she goes on looking at him in the lamp until he’s the one who has to look away.
He gets the coat open on the floorboards under her and the shirt off her shoulders and kneels over her in the doorway, and he tells her.

He has never said anything like it to anybody. He doesn’t dress it. He says it in Youngstown words, short ones, with his mouth barely off her skin. Her mouth, he tells her, and puts his on it. The back of her neck, here, under the hair, where it’s warm — and he turns her face aside with his hand and puts his mouth there, and she shivers the length of her body. Her hands. The weight of her asleep. The sound she makes when he touches her like this — and he does, and she makes it, and he says, “That one. That one,” into her ear, and her hips come up off the coat.
“Keep going,” she says. Her eyes are shut. “You never *say* things. You say *I’m good*. Don’t you dare stop talking.”

So he doesn’t. He tells her about the phone at two in the morning on his chest in 412, warm from her voice. He tells her he missed her feet on him at night, always freezing, two packages straight out of the icebox, and she laughs with her eyes shut and puts them on him now to prove it. He tells her what he wanted on that motel tile. He tells her the thing he missed most: how she says his name, low, when she’s close, all one breath — and she goes red from her collarbones up to the dark hair, he can see it even in the gray from the window, and she gets his jeans open and pulls him down onto her by the hips.

He keeps talking when he’s inside her. He didn’t know he could do that until he does it, his mouth at her ear: how long two weeks is, that he loves her, that she’s here. She answers with her body before she answers with anything else. She wraps her legs around him and holds on to the back of his neck, and the boards knock under them, and her breathing comes apart into pieces, and then she says it, just as he told her he missed it, his name, low and all in one breath —

— and that’s the end of what he can say. It goes through both of them close together, her first, crying out against his shoulder, and him into her hair a moment after, and he holds her through it with his arms under her and the sheepskin bunched in his fists.
They lie in the doorway, breathing like they ran there. The record goes on downstairs.
“You talk now,” she says, into his collarbone. “When did you start talking?”
“Tuesday. Behind a dumpster.”

s16a.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 1:05 AM · HER ROOM — STORIES FROM THE SET

journal.title: Debbie Callender
journal.text: Skye’s mother. Her manager. A voice like a hotel lobby. Did a Chevy commercial in ’94. Calls her baby. Keeps a legal pad. ‘Then you’re going to be very expensive.’ Tuesday, Studio City: already up, already asking about Teddy. ‘Baby. A *bed*.’ The accountant in Encino called her about Haiti: ‘Sweetheart, *I’m* Skylark.’ At the valet, with no lobby in it: Skye doesn’t write to anybody. She doesn’t write to her. In Santa Fe she took the room next door from the thirteenth and sat in video village. She asked for a softer take, for Cassidy’s girls. The director let Skye choose. Skye chose mean. That night in the motel Debbie cried, and said it was the best thing she’s ever seen her do, and that it terrified her. Corinne called about the faith-journey sit-down. Skye let it ring.

body: By one in the morning they’ve made it onto the mattress, under the blanket, with the sheepskin spread over the top for weight. The record downstairs ran out an hour ago.

body.text: The lamp is still on from the doorway, down on the floor in its paper shade, throwing the two of them up the wall.

body: What’s left is the surf at the foot of the bluff and her chewing. She sent him down to the hall table for the Pop-Tarts — brown sugar cinnamon, from the vending machine outside the motel office, carried a thousand miles in a coat pocket and gone flat on one side where she sat on them in Phoenix — and up on the way back for the sweatshirt off the rail, and she checks it before she’ll put it on, collar to her nose.
“*Washed*,” she says, with real surprise, and gets into it.
Then she tells him. She tells it with the parts played: lying on her back with the Pop-Tart held up over her face, crumbs coming down on the sweatshirt, doing the voices for the room.

“Day two, the horse bit the director. Clementine. On the *shoulder*, through a down vest, in front of the crew.” The director, a small woman, being very calm: “*Okay.*” Then a very calm walk to her car, and ten minutes sitting in it. “So after that I made friends with her. On my own time. I stole carrots off craft services every morning and stood in her stall at six with my coat full of them and talked to her about my mother.”
“What did she say?”

“She ate the carrots. She’s a wonderful listener.” A bite. “Dell has to ride her into the yard at a lope and get down without ever looking at her. And I wanted to look at her. So I made friends with her, so Dell didn’t have to.”
The director is Ana Lucero. Ana asked her, the first week, who Dell was with.

“Nobody ever asks that. On *Sweetwater* nobody asks Cassidy anything but where she got the sweater.” She turns her head on the pillow. “I told her. The boy. The one her father put in the back of his car.” She licks sugar off her thumb. “And Ana *kept* it. She put it in. There’s a shot of a pickup going by the kitchen window, and Dell not looking at it. Two seconds. Not one person watching will ever know what that is.” The Pop-Tart comes down and points at him. “I know.”

Walt Breedlove played the sheriff: sixty-some, a face like a saddle left out, forty Westerns, shot by every leading man who ever wore a hat. On the last day, by the honey wagon, he took her by the elbow. It’s the voice from the red light, gentled down: an old man being careful with her. “*You’re not a nice girl, kid. You’re a kind one. Different muscle.*”
Jack lies with his hand on her ankle under the blanket and doesn’t say anything, because she’s gone quiet after it, looking up past him with the Pop-Tart forgotten on her chest.

“And the crew clapped,” she says. “The first time I said *Out* and got it right. The boom guy started it. And a grip who was on *Sweetwater* in season one, who hated me then. I know he did, I heard him say so to the craft-services lady. He clapped the longest.”
“Which take?”

“The barn. Walt says *Your mother called*, and I say *Out*, and then I don’t leave. I just stand there in the door with the horse behind me. Ana didn’t call cut. She let it run till the horse got bored.”
She wrote Danny, small, with capitals. “He told me,” Jack says. “THE GOAT AT CARRILLO.”
“I told him other things.”
“What other things?”
“That you stall.”

Valentine’s Day she went to Mass by herself, at the cathedral in Santa Fe, St. Francis: big, brown stone, cold, candles banked up everywhere, old women in black lace who knew every word without the book. She sat in the back.

body.text: “I didn’t go up. I’ve never known how, and anyway, I figured you were going up for both of us.”
body.else: “I didn’t go up. Because you don’t.” She looks at the Pop-Tart as though it might know. “Is that allowed? To not go up because somebody else doesn’t?”

body: “And then the Gospel.” She comes up on one elbow. “Jack. There’s a woe for people everybody likes. *Woe to you when all speak well of you.* It’s right there in it.” She aims the Pop-Tart at his chest. “I’m *in* the Bible.”

He laughs. He gets about halfway through it before he sees her face. It isn’t laughing, not all the way down. Somebody in Burbank is paid by the hour to make sure all speak well of Skye Callender. He stops laughing and keeps his hand where it is on her ankle, and she lies back down, and after a minute she goes on to the ashes.

Rosalind, the makeup girl, the one who wiped hers off for continuity — Rosalind is from Española and goes to Mass every day of her life, and she kept her own ashes on all day under her bangs. She combed them down over it in the trailer mirror. “Where continuity couldn’t see,” Skye says. “I want to be Rosalind when I grow up.”
“You’d make a terrible Rosalind. You’d tell everybody.”
“I’d tell *you*.”
“When do you hear? About the show.”

“May. They’ll tell us in May.” She puts the last corner of the first Pop-Tart in her mouth and tears open the second foil with her teeth, as if May were a town she’d driven through once and didn’t think much of.

And her mother. Debbie took the room next door from the thirteenth, with the connecting door, and sat every day in video village beside the monitors with her legal pad on her knee. On the fourth day she asked Ana for a softer take of the kitchen scene — “for Cassidy’s girls,” Skye says, in her mother’s vowels exactly, “the ones who write in, the twelve-year-olds in Tulsa” — and Ana let Skye choose. Skye chose mean. That night Debbie stood in the doorway between the rooms in her robe and cried, and told her it was the best thing she had ever seen her do, and that it terrified her. Corinne called the next morning about the faith-journey sit-down. Skye watched it ring on the motel bedspread till it stopped.
She’s quiet after that. She folds the foil over the last of the Pop-Tart, very neatly, into a square.
“She said it terrified her.”
The surf comes in and goes over at the bottom of the bluff.
“I think she meant me.”

Jack puts his arm under her and pulls her over onto his chest, and she goes, and lies there. In a while she unfolds the foil and eats the rest of the Pop-Tart over his heart, getting crumbs on both of them.

s16b.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 2:40 AM · HER ROOM — THE WEDNESDAYS
body: “Your turn,” she says, at twenty to three, into his chest. “I told you the *horse*. You haven’t told me one thing that happened to you in two weeks that wasn’t somebody else’s snow.”

He could tell her about the futon, or Kevin’s candle. She’s had most of it already, by text, in pieces, at a quarter a picture. He lies with her weight on him and the surf coming up the bluff, and what he wants to tell her isn’t any of that. He shifts so he can see her face. The Christmas bulbs over the window are still up and still dark. It’s Lent; somebody ought to take them down.

body.text: So he tells her about Wednesdays. That he went back the Wednesday after she left and knelt on a strip of gaffer tape and told the man behind the linen all of it, Friday night and the two doors he walked past after, and said he meant to stop, and meant it. That he went up at Mass on Valentine’s, and again on Wednesday with the ash still on him. That he kept it ten days. That tonight he didn’t, and he’ll go this Wednesday and say so, because that is how it works, you go back and say what happened. That he dreads the Wednesday and wants it.
body.else: So he tells her about Wednesdays. That he went back the Wednesday after she left and knelt on a strip of gaffer tape and told the man behind the linen the truth, and went again this Wednesday with ash on his forehead and told it again. That the truth is he can’t promise. That without the promise there’s no absolution, only a blessing, and a man on the other side of the linen who says *come back*, and he does. That this is why he stays in the pew on Sundays. That he’ll stay in it today, in about nine hours.

body: He doesn’t make a speech of it. He tells it with his hand moving in the dark hair at the back of her head, in the order it happened, and when he runs out he stops. She doesn’t interrupt him once. Her hand on his chest closes on a fistful of blanket somewhere in the middle and opens again, and that’s all.

body.text: She’s quiet a long time on his shoulder. “So on Wednesday you told a man you wouldn’t,” she says. “And then I got off a plane.”
body.else: She’s quiet a long time on his shoulder. “So every Wednesday,” she says, “you go tell a man you’re not sorry enough about me.”

choices.text: “I go tell him the truth. It’s the only clean thing I’ve got left.”
choices.key: When Skye asked about Wednesdays, you told her the truth is the only clean thing you’ve got left.
response: “Clean.” She says the word back and turns it over, carefully, like something she found in a coat pocket and isn’t sure is hers. Nothing in her face is angry. He would rather it were. She lifts her head off his shoulder to see his face.
“Am I the thing that isn’t?”
“No.”
It’s true, and he says it so she can hear that it’s true, and she hears it. It doesn’t fix anything. He can see that on her, and he can see her see it on him.
She puts her head back down on his shoulder and leaves her hand where it was.

choices.text: “I’m not sorry about you. I’m sorry I can’t be two things at once.”
choices.key: When Skye asked about Wednesdays, you told her you’re not sorry about her — you’re sorry you can’t be two things at once.
response: She says it back under her breath, against his shoulder, trying the weight of it — *two things at once* — as she runs a new line at a red light to see whether it will hold. It holds. He can feel it hold, and he can feel it hurt her on the way in.
“Then what am I?” she says. “On Wednesdays.”
“You’re the reason I go.”
She lies with that. Her breath goes out slow across his chest, and comes back, and he can’t tell yet whether he’s given her something good. He isn’t sure himself.
“That’s a good line,” she says at last. “I hate it.” She doesn’t move off him.

choices.key: When Skye asked about Wednesdays, you said yes.
response: It lands on her like a slap. The breath goes out of her, and she sits up with the blanket held against her, her back to him in his sweatshirt, and for a while the only thing in the room is the surf.
Then, without turning around: “Thank you for not lying.”
And, after another set has come in and gone over: “Am I the thing you’re sorry for?”
“No,” he says, to her back. It’s the part after *yes*, and he can tell from the line of her shoulders that it isn’t getting to her yet.
She stays sitting up. But her hand comes back behind her and finds his on the blanket by feel, and takes it, and keeps it.

s16c.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 3:20 AM · HER ROOM — THE SECOND TIME

body.text: “Clean,” she says again, later, and puts it down.
“Two things at once,” she says, later, like a note she means to keep.
Later she lies back down, on her own side of the mattress, and then not on her own side.

body: She doesn’t leave it there. She lies on her side facing him with her hand under her cheek and asks him how it works. Really. Not the book.
“What do you say? When you go in. The actual words.”

He tells her. *Bless me, Father.* How long it’s been. Then the thing, in as few words as it takes and no fewer, on a kneeler with tape on it, to a square of linen with a man’s shape behind it and a radiator going. What comes back through the linen he mostly keeps; it was said to him. He gives her the part he can’t help carrying up the hill: *come back*.
“Is it worse now? Because it’s Lent?”
He thinks about it honestly. “It’s the same. Lent’s just when you notice.”
She takes that in. A car goes by down on Del Playa with its windows open and a party in it, and goes on.
“And Sundays,” she says. “When everybody goes up. What do you do?”
“Kneel. Watch them go.”
“What do I do?”
“Whatever you want. Sit. Kneel. Read the hymnal.”
“I’ll kneel,” she says. “I like the kneeling. It’s the only part where I know my blocking.”
“Does he know the other one?”
“He knows Skye. When I pray for you, I use the other one.”
He feels her smile against his shoulder. “Good. Keep the other one.”
“I’m keeping it.”
“Can I come? Sunday.” She hears herself. “Today.”
“It’s at eleven-thirty.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
“Yes,” he says. “Come.”
“Is he kind to you? Your priest.”
“He’s kind. He doesn’t let me off.”
“Good,” she says, into his shoulder. “Don’t let him let you off.”

body.text: She reaches over him and turns off the lamp.
body.else: She reaches over him and turns on the lamp.

body: It’s nothing like the doorway. It’s slow, and almost nothing is said. She comes over him under the blanket with the sheepskin’s weight on her back and takes him into her and stays there, barely moving, her forearms on the pillow on either side of his head and her face a few inches over his. He puts his hand into the dark hair at the back of her skull and holds it. Under the dye it’s the same warm nape, the same small hollow behind her ear his thumb goes to on its own. They move like that a long time, hardly at all, like two people trying not to wake a house. The hurt from before is still in her face. She lets him see it and keeps her eyes on his, and he keeps his on hers, and what they do is slow enough that he can feel every bit of her around him, and her heartbeat in it, and his own. When she’s close her eyes fill and don’t spill over.
“Mary Catherine,” he says.

She breathes against his mouth, and his name is in it. It comes up in both of them slowly, a long swell that lifts and lifts and sets them down, and she doesn’t make a sound until after, and then it’s only his name again, into his neck.

She sleeps on him. Her breathing goes long and then longer, and catches once, the small hitch she makes going under, and then she’s gone. The surf comes up the bluff and goes back. His arm is under her, and somewhere past three-thirty it goes to pins and needles from the shoulder down, and then to nothing at all, and he leaves it where it is.

s17.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S — FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT
s17.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days”
body: They make the 11:30 with four minutes to spare, which by Skye’s clock is early. The morning hasn’t made up its mind: a high white overcast with some warmth leaking through it, and the eucalyptus along Ocean Road letting go of last night’s fog one fat drop at a time onto the sidewalk and the back of his neck. Inside St. Brendan’s, Lent has been in since Wednesday. The flowers are gone from the altar, the brass stands pushed back against the wall. There’s violet on the ambo, and a bare stretch of tile in front of the tabernacle where the ferns used to be.

body.text: She came in a navy dress from the bottom of the suitcase, still creased in a grid from the fold, with his flannel over it unbuttoned and the sheepskin over both. No hat. In Sol’s front hall, with her hand already on the doorknob, she picked it up off the floor where it had spent the night, turned it over, and set it on the newel post. “It’s not baptized,” she said. The flannel she kept. “The flannel’s been to Mass. It knows what to do.”
body.else: She came in a navy dress from the bottom of the suitcase, still creased in a grid from the fold, with his flannel over it unbuttoned and the sheepskin over both. No hat. In Sol’s front hall, with her hand already on the doorknob, she lifted it off the newel post and turned it over and hung it back. “It’s not baptized,” she said. The flannel she kept. “The flannel’s been to Mass. It knows what to do.”

body: He goes to the Joseph side, halfway back, where he sits now, and she follows him in without a word about it and takes the inside. He has the aisle and nowhere to go.

Gus Ferreira gives the organ one long low chord, and the choir starts the entrance hymn, an old plain tune in four lines that walks instead of marching, and the procession comes up the center aisle: the cross, two servers with candles, the lector with the big book held up, Father Osei in violet. Skye stands when everybody stands. She has the missalette open to the right page before he does, and she doesn’t sing, but she reads along with her lips. After the Kyrie the place where the Gloria goes is just quiet, and the whole church sits down into it. Before the Gospel the cantor sings something about glory and praise, and there’s no Alleluia, and Jack’s ear keeps going back to where it should be, like a tongue to a missing tooth.

Osei reads it himself. Jesus *led by the Spirit into the desert for forty days*, and hungry at the end of them. The stones, the bread. *One does not live on bread alone.* The kingdoms of the world from a high place, and the parapet of the Temple, and the last line. Osei reads it slower than the rest: *When the devil had finished every temptation, he departed from him for a time.*
He closes the book and stands at the ambo with nothing in his hands.

“He is led there,” he says. “Notice that. The Spirit leads him, and the Spirit is not in the habit of losing people. In Scripture the desert is where God takes his own when he wants them to himself. Hosea says it of Israel, the way a husband would: *I will lead her into the desert and speak to her heart.* So if you find yourself somewhere dry this Lent — and you will; it is the season for it — do not be too quick to decide you were sent away. You may have been brought. Forty days is an appointment, not a sentence.” A pause, and then: “And read the last line before you get comfortable. The devil leaves him *for a time*. Even the Gospel admits there is a sequel.”
He sits down.
Skye leans over until her mouth is at his ear. “I was *in* a desert,” she whispers. “Two weeks. Nobody spoke to my heart. A horse bit a director.” Jack studies his shoes until it passes.

She comes in late on the Creed, on the parts she has, like somebody who knows the chorus and not the verses, and goes quiet on the rest and listens to the rest. At the consecration she kneels when he kneels, and keeps her eyes where his are.

Ten pews up on the Mary side there’s a dark head he knows, back from New Orleans, her hair up and the oatmeal cardigan. At Communion she goes up with her row. He sees it fast, all of it at once, and then he’s looking at the hymnal, at a hymn they’ve already sung.

The usher reaches their pew and stops at the end of it with his hand turned out, and the family beside them — a father, a mother, a boy of nine in a clip-on tie — say excuse me and edge out past their knees into the aisle. Jack stays where he is. Skye doesn’t get up either. The usher looks at the two of them, kindly, and moves along to the next pew. This week they pass the plate over both of them.

body.text: Last Sunday he went up from this side of the church. This Sunday the family goes past him.

body: So she watches. The line goes up the center aisle at its Sunday crawl and comes back down the side, past the end of their pew, close enough to touch: the boy in the clip-on tie with his hands folded the way the nuns showed somebody once, two girls in Marisol rowing jackets, an old man with a cane who stops to genuflect and takes his time getting back up, a nurse in blue scrubs on her way to a shift with her hands crossed over her badge. Skye looks at each face as it comes back down, carefully, one at a time, like she’s trying to see where they’ve put it.
Her hand comes over onto his on the back of the pew in front of them. Her fingers go down between his. She keeps them there until the last of the line has gone by.
Jack prays for her by name. He uses the one she was baptized with.

On the way out he wets his fingers in the font and turns and holds them out to her, and she looks at him and then touches her fingertips to his and crosses herself, right to left, then fixes it. On the table beside the font are the stacks of bulletins, a carton of Lenten rice bowls folded flat, and a fat green paperback with an index card taped across its cover.

Outside, Osei is at the top of the steps in the white light, in violet, shaking hands. He takes Skye’s hand first. “Good morning,” he says, and looks at her face with attention, a polite moment and no more, and lets her go. Then Jack’s hand, dry and warm. “Good morning.” It’s exactly the handshake he gives the family behind them, and the one he’ll give the man with the cane, and Jack is grateful to the soles of his feet to be nobody in particular.

They go down Ocean Road under the eucalyptus with the drops coming down on them. She has his arm. She doesn’t say anything for a block, and Skye not saying anything for a block is an event: the stucco houses with their red tile, a sprinkler going on somebody’s lawn in February, a kid on a skateboard taking the hill in a long clattering curve, the sea under the bluffs on the right, gray this morning. At the corner where Ocean Road gives out into Del Playa she stops under the stop sign and turns him around by the arm to face her.
“Then explain it to me,” she says. “Until I understand.”

choices.key: When Skye asked you to explain it until she understood, you told her to start anywhere.
response: She takes his arm again and starts them walking, down Del Playa toward the house, past a recycling bin of red cups tipped over in the gutter.
“Then start with the bread,” she says. “That’s the one you won’t go up for.”
She says it gently. It goes in anyway, and he lets it, and walks her home.

choices.text: “It’s two thousand years long. Bring snacks.”
choices.key: When Skye asked you to explain it until she understood, you told her to bring snacks.
response: “I brought Pop-Tarts.”

She has. Out of the coat pocket comes one more foil pack — she bought out the machine — flat as a letter. She tears it open with her teeth, gives him half, and takes his arm and steps off the curb into Del Playa.
“Start with the bread,” she says, with her mouth full.

choices.text: “I don’t understand all of it either.”
choices.key: When Skye asked you to explain it until she understood, you told her you don’t understand all of it either.
response: She looks up at him under the stop sign. Her face eases.

“Good,” she says. “Then we’ll be wrong together. That’s a scene.” She tucks her hand back through his arm and waits for the kid on the skateboard to clatter past them and away down the hill. “Start with the bread.”
They step off the curb together into Del Playa.

s18.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 4:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — USA–CANADA
body: The sun at twenty to five comes in level off the Channel and straight through the Fishbowl’s glass, and from the lobby the lounge is a tank of gold with people in it: the backs of heads over the couch, steam off somebody’s cocoa, Doug Pruitt on his feet in front of the television with his hand over his heart. The anthem is coming out of five speakers he carried down from 420 himself.
At the foot of the stairs Jack makes his pitch with one hand on the rail. “Theo’s MacBook is upstairs. Four-twelve. Two people and a laptop, and no chanting.”

Skye is already turning toward the glass. “I’ve been in a motel with a horse for two weeks,” she says. “I want a *room*.” She has the door open while he’s still standing there holding the plan, and the anthem comes out at them across the carpet with all its brass, and she pulls him in by the sleeve of the Carhartt, past Priya’s laminate on the glass. Doug turns from the screen with his hand still on his heart. “Dude,” he says, at a volume that reaches the window. “*New Mexico’s back.*”

The Logitech has been liberated from 420 for the duration and wired in under the TV cart, the subwoofer squatting on the carpet like a footlocker, the speaker wire taped down in long silver stripes. Taped to the cart, at Doug’s eye level:

body.title: Taped to the TV cart, the Fishbowl
body.text:
TEMPORARY A/V INSTALLATION — APPROVED
For the duration of the XXI Olympic Winter Games ONLY.
All wire to be taped DOWN.
— P. Raman, RA, 4th floor
(Doug: this means the subwoofer too.)

body: The anthem ends. Doug takes his hand off his heart and starts in under his breath, through his teeth, on a technicality: “U. S. A. U. S. A.” Priya looks up from her table by the door. He goes on mouthing it.

Forty-one seconds after the puck drops, an American defenseman named Rafalski puts one in from the point, and the Fishbowl goes up. Doug is standing on the couch cushions with both arms in the air. Priya stands to object, finds that the Handbook has nothing on this, and sits back down.
Theo has the near end of the couch, loafers crossed on the coffee table, the only man in the room betting against his own country. “I have a burrito on Canada,” he tells them. “On principle.”
“What principle?” says Skye.
“Universal health care and a better class of apology.” He looks up at her from under his eyebrows. “Callender.”
“Ted.”

Yusuf, cross-legged on the carpet at Theo’s feet, holds the other end of the burrito and has written the terms on the back of his hand in ballpoint. Kevin and Clare have the loveseat. Clare is in a Sharks cap, explaining icing to Doug for the third time, now with a napkin for the rink and a sugar packet for the puck. “My brother Javi plays club,” she tells him. “I’ve been explaining icing to boys since I could talk.”
“So it’s like offsides,” Doug says.
“It is not like offsides.”
“It’s like *diet* offsides.”
Margot has the armchair and a thesis. “It’s a cold war,” she says, “fought by dentists’ sons.”

And at the far table under the window, where the gold comes in strongest, Laney has her boots up on a second chair and Lena has a paperback flat under one hand and a pencil in the other. She has read straight through the anthem.

Skye goes around the room in order: Margot first, who allows herself to be hugged in the armchair with her arms at her sides; Kevin, who stands up to be hugged and then doesn’t know when to sit down; Clare, who says *Oh!* and hugs back hard; Doug from behind, and he yells. She doesn’t let go of Jack’s hand for any of it, so he goes too, around the couch and past the TV cart, toward the window.

As they come past the far table Lena looks up from the book. “Welcome back,” she says to Skye — her mother’s manners, Mémère’s maybe, warm enough to be real — and Skye says, “Thank you. It’s good to be back,” and Lena’s eyes go down to the page again, and the pencil moves. Nothing to Jack. Not a look he could prove.

It was courteous, and it was for Skye, and it was the right thing to say to a girl home from two weeks away. Jack is at the pop machine by the door with a dollar half into the slot and no memory of the carpet in between. The machine takes the dollar, thinks it over, and gives it back.
From the far table Laney calls across the room, all honey, “Skye, darlin’, you look like a whole Western,” and Skye touches the brim of a hat she isn’t wearing.

Then Laney is at his elbow. Doug’s Igloo sits on the carpet beside the machine, full of ice and not much else, and she bends to it and goes through the ice with her bare hand, choosing the last Diet Coke as if it had wronged her. When she speaks it’s the first thing she has said out loud to him since the curb, and she says it low, so it carries exactly as far as he is.

body.text: “Seminar tables are slick, fireman. Things slide.”
“Check your mail lately, fireman?”
“Nice handwriting, fireman.”
“Some people answer their mail, fireman.”
“I turned nineteen, by the way,” she adds. “In case the fourth floor didn’t carry it.”

body: She straightens up with the can, and she’s back at the far table with her boots on the chair before he has anything.
On the loveseat Clare has turned right around to Kevin and is thanking him in front of the room:

body.text: “Thank you for the roses. You signed it *Kevin*. Just Kevin. I liked that.”
“Thank you for the strings. Nobody has ever got the gauge right. Not even my grandfather.”
“Thank you for the letter.” She lets that go by a moment. “I’ve read it more than once.”
“My brothers told me they voted. Thank you for the jersey. And the chocolates. Javi says the chocolates were the minority report.”

body: Kevin looks at the floor, and once, across the room, at Jack, and back down at the floor.
“Dude,” Doug says, with the Igloo’s lid up. “We’re *out*. Who’s got legs?”

Skye has her coat over her arm and is standing in the middle of the carpet looking for where the two of them go. There’s the orange chair by the door, with its back to the glass and a cigarette burn in one arm from some year before Priya. There’s the middle of the couch, where Theo has moved his loafers over to make a place, dead in front of the screen with the window just past it. “There,” Skye says, and points at the couch.

response: He takes the orange chair by the door instead. Skye follows him over and sits on the arm of it with her boots in his lap and the sheepskin over the both of them. She doesn’t say a word about the couch. From here the screen is a little sideways and the room is between him and the window, and he can see every bit of the game he needs to.

choices.text: *The middle of the couch, where Skye wants it.*
response: The middle of the couch, then. Skye tucks in against him under the sheepskin like it’s a blanket at a drive-in, her dark head on his shoulder, Theo’s loafers back up on the coffee table on one side and Margot’s armchair on the other. The screen is dead ahead. Just past its left edge, under the window, is the far table, and a pencil moving at it. He watches the game harder than anybody has ever watched hockey. By the end of the period he understands icing.

choices.text: *Volunteer for a pop run and take the long way.*
response: “I’ll go.” He takes orders. Doug: “Mountain Dew, dude, it’s *patriotic*.” Theo, a ginger ale, “in a glass bottle, if Delgado has evolved.” Skye, root beer. He takes the long way, down through the basement and past the laundry, the sweet chemical heat of it and the dryer at the end of the row standing open with nobody’s sweatshirt in it, to the machine by the boiler room that still takes dollars.

He comes back up with his arms full of cans to find the room on its feet again. He has missed Rafalski’s second. Doug narrates it to him in full, on the coffee table, with the cans: the Mountain Dew is Rafalski, the ginger ale is the Canadian goalie, and the root beer, tragically, is the puck.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. s18a.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 6:30 PM · THE FISHBOWL — THE THIRD PERIOD
body: At the second intermission the far table empties. Lena closes the paperback on the pencil and puts it under her arm, and Laney stands and slides her arm through Lena’s, and they go.

body.text: They go out past his chair, close enough that Lena’s cardigan sleeve all but brushes his knee, and Laney’s perfume comes after them, something with vanilla in it. They don’t slow. He watches the Zamboni on the screen going around on the clean ice until the glass door has swung shut behind them.

He doesn’t see them go. He knows they’ve gone because the sightline has: the far table is just a table at the edge of the screen, two empty chairs and a wet ring on the Formica where a can stood, and his shoulders come down an inch he didn’t know they were up.

He’s on cans again by then, by acclamation, and he meets them on the basement stairs coming up with his arms full. Laney says, “And our next contestant is room service.” Lena says nothing, and goes up on the far side of the rail.

body: The third period belongs to the American goalie. His name is Miller, and he stands in his crease in Vancouver and gets shot at by the entire nation of Canada from every angle there is, and stops it, and stops it. Yusuf, on the carpet, has started counting the saves out loud without anybody asking him to, carrying the total over from the first two periods. “Thirty-eight,” he says, to no one. “Thirty-nine.” Theo, whose burrito is going down with every number, asks him to stop. “Forty.”

Late, Canada gets one back, and the room goes so quiet that the subwoofer is the loudest thing in it: the crowd in Vancouver coming up through the carpet like weather. Clare has both hands over her mouth. Kevin has a thumbnail in his teeth. By the door Priya has risen to her feet and doesn’t seem to know it. “Forty-one,” says Yusuf. “Forty-two.”

With under a minute left Canada pulls its goalie for the extra man, and the net at the far end of the ice stands empty, and an American named Kesler chases down a loose puck and puts it in the empty net, and that’s the game. USA 5, Canada 3.

The Fishbowl goes up. Doug is on the arm of the couch with his arms straight up like a referee. “Douglas,” Priya says. “Handbook.” Priya’s laminate has come unstuck from the glass in the uproar and slid down onto the carpet, and Priya isn’t picking it up. Clare is pounding Kevin on the shoulder with her fist, and Kevin is letting her. Theo stands and pays Yusuf a burrito with a ten-dollar bill and dignity. Margot remarks that nobody has asked her opinion.

Jack is on his feet with the rest of them, yelling at a hockey game, a sport he did not know the rules of at four o’clock. Skye comes up on her toes in front of him and takes his face in both her hands and kisses him, hard, laughing into it, in the middle of the carpet with Doug’s chant coming down on them from the arm of the couch. Then she ducks her head and puts it under his chin, the dark hair, no hat, still smelling of motel shampoo, and he gets both arms around her and the sheepskin and lifts her a little off the floor, and he’s happy, all at once and at the top of his voice, with a hockey game going and her mouth tasting of Swiss Miss.

Over her head he watches Priya pick her laminate up off the carpet, read it, and lay it on her table, words down. Doug starts the chant again from the arm of the couch, and the room takes it up, and somewhere in it, under her breath, so does Priya.

s19.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 21 · 8:30 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE BACK BOOTH
body: Sunday night at the Anchor is three fishermen at the counter with their caps on, the jukebox dark, and Rudy’s transistor on the shelf over the flattop with a ballgame on it in Spanish, a crowd the size of a thumbnail going up and coming down. On a Sunday Jack comes in the front door like a customer, and from this side of the pass the kitchen looks smaller.

He asked them in the lobby after the game, one at a time, by name: Theo, Kevin, Margot. Clare had quartet. So it’s the five of them in the back booth, Skye on the inside against the window and Jack on the outside with his knee against hers under the table, and the front door in the corner of his eye. Margot notices. “You’ve taken the seat with the egress, Costigan,” she says, opening her menu. “I’m filing it under avoidant.”
Gloria arrives with the menus under her arm and the pencil out of her hair, and stops at the end of the booth with her weight on one hip, and gives Skye a good long look.

body.text: “The peach,” she says. “You owe me a verdict on the lattice.”
body.else: “So you’re why I gave him Saturday,” she says.

body: The chalkboard over the pie case says APPLE — LATTICE in Gloria’s capitals. She brings a slice before anybody has ordered one and sets it down in front of Skye with the fork standing up in it.

Skye sits up for it. She cuts a corner with the side of the fork, looks at the cross-hatching, eats it slowly with her eyes shut, and opens them on Gloria. “Showing off on top,” she says. “Honest underneath.”
Gloria puts the pencil behind her ear and turns to Jack, delighted. “That’s what I said about *him*. Backwards.”
Skye looks at Jack. Jack looks at the pie. He rates it a seven, to change the subject, and Gloria says that’s generous from a man with his record, and goes for the coffee.

Theo and Skye are doing Los Angeles across the table at each other. Debbie threw the crew a party in the motel courtyard the night before the wrap, with a rented chocolate fountain that froze solid at seven thousand feet and had to be served with a chisel. Theo counters with his mother, who once threw a party to apologize for a party.
“Two women,” Theo says, “who throw parties as policy.”
“Foreign policy,” says Skye.
“Domestic. It’s worse.”
Margot has her notebook out and is interviewing Skye about Dell for what she calls a footnote. “Is she likable?”
“God, no.”
“Does she smile?”
“Once. At the horse. Ana cut it.”
Margot writes that down. “Refusing likability is a political act.”
Skye points her fork at her across the table. “She just doesn’t like her dad’s questions.”

Kevin is eating his coffee cake carefully, as if it might be taken back. “Clare asked me to come hear her play next Sunday, at the five-thirty,” he says, cutting a corner off. “I go anyway. She asked anyway.” He looks over at Jack and then down at his fork again, and he’s smiling at the fork.

Jack catches Theo watching him. Theo has his cup halfway up and is looking across the booth at Jack with Skye’s head on his shoulder and her boot hooked around his ankle under the table, and he keeps looking, long enough that Jack sees him see it. Then he sets the cup down in its saucer.
“Kevin,” Theo says. “Picture it. The Newman spring retreat. A silent one. At a vineyard.”
“Respectfully, no.”
“Silence, Tran. Grapes. A sommelier who has taken a vow.”

Margot says she would attend a silent retreat only as an ethnographer. Skye says she’ll go if there’s a horse. Kevin says there will be no horse, and no vineyard, and no retreat, and Theo writes VINEYARD on a napkin and puts it in his breast pocket, where Jack has seen a lot of ideas go to wait.
Gloria comes back with the pot and fills Skye’s cup first, and stands there with it to tell her the hair is a crime and it suits her.
“It washes out,” Skye says. “Twelve washes.”
“Don’t hurry it, hon.”

In the lot after, Skye has the Saab running for the heater and both hands on the wheel, and she doesn’t put it in gear. Through the windshield the Anchor’s front window is yellow, and inside it Gloria is putting the chairs up on the tables, one by one, legs in the air. Skye watches her do three of them.
“You’ve been arranging rooms all day.”

body.text: “Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then the chair by the door. Then this booth, with the door on your side.”
“Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then you sat in the middle of that couch like it was going to bite you.”
“Four-twelve, with a laptop. Then a pop run through the *basement*. Then this booth, with the door on your side.”

body: She says it easily, with her head back against the rest and the dash lights green along the side of her face, and her eyes on him, and then she waits.

choices.key: When Skye said you’d been arranging rooms all day, you told her Laney’s mad at you.
response: It’s true. It isn’t all of it.

“Laney’s mad at you in very good manners,” Skye says. “That’s the expensive kind.” She seems to find that the right size. “Okay.” She puts the Saab in reverse, one arm across the back of his seat, looking out the rear window past his ear, and backs them out under the light.

choices.key: When Skye said you’d been arranging rooms all day, you told her you wanted her to yourself.
response: That’s true too.

She takes it. She leans across the gearshift and kisses him, slow, with the engine going and the heater blowing on their knees, and when she sits back she’s smiling, and whatever else there is stays outside in the lot with the dumpster and the gulls.

choices.text: “Theo taught me seating. It’s a sickness.”
response: She laughs, with her head back against the rest, a real laugh that fogs a little patch of the windshield. She looks over at him. “Picture it,” she says, in a cashmere voice that is Theo’s to the vowel, “a man who seats his girlfriend by the exits.” And she puts it in first and drives.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Tuesday morning she had the day girl’s shift. Hale sat in our booth till two Sunday morning reading her Housman; she put him in a cab. Theo pitched me New Orleans on her placemats. She rated it a meringue: all air, and it still costs four dollars. She gave me Saturday the twentieth off. Go get your peach; Rudy’ll cover the Hobart. Rudy said no. Sunday night the peach rated her lattice: showing off on top, honest underneath. Gloria said that’s what she said about me, backwards.

s20.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 22 · 7:15 AM · CAMPUS POINT — PAIR FORTY-ONE
body: The sun is half an hour up out of the Channel, low and yellow and in their eyes, and the Point is breaking where it does: long glassy lefts peeling off the reef in sets, nobody on them yet but one gull riding the backs of the swells in and back out. The air smells of kelp and wet ice plant. Oceanography meets Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven. This is Monday at a quarter past seven, because she wanted to see where he counted.

She sits on the bench at the edge of the bluff in the sheepskin with the collar up and the clipboard on her knees, and the department stopwatch on its shoelace around her neck, PROPERTY OF MORRO 1100. Under the clip are his two weeks: every form, in order, his square capitals down both columns. She reads all of them, every column, and doesn’t skip.
“You measured the waves without me.”
“Somebody had to.”

body: She laughs at the water. “He’s *funny*. “That’s a wave.”
“It has a tail.”
“It’s breaking.”
