body: The fog that came in off the Point at noon has stayed, and the light in the windows of 302 is the same flat white from the radiator to the clock. There’s no slab of sun on the varnish today. The table hasn’t got a bright end and a dark one. It has two ends.

The chairs have been rearranged by attrition. Caleb got here at twenty to one and took the last seat at the window end, the one that sat empty in the sun all the eleventh, and isn’t giving it back. “It has a better view of the door,” he says, when nobody has asked. That puts Lena two seats from the end, between Caleb and the window girl with the library copy that crackles. Yusuf has the corner and a lidded coffee. Evan has the roster and the radiator, and a Commons cup he holds in both hands for the heat. Jack has the door end and the clock, as before, and a used paperback from the campus bookstore, four dollars and fifty cents, with somebody else’s yellow highlighter all the way through the air raid and nowhere after it.

At the window end Lena has an old orange Penguin open flat under her left hand and a pencil in her right. She hasn’t looked down the table. He knows because he hasn’t either. She has been back four days: Thursday at the curb from a stairwell window, Sunday at the 11:30 on the Mary side, Sunday afternoon in the Fishbowl saying welcome back to somebody else. He has the list, and he resents every line of it.

Hale comes in with his coat over his arm and his own copy bristling with torn strips of envelope, and takes the middle of the long side, where he can turn his head for either end. He turns it both ways, slowly, checking the traffic.

“The chair has had a restful fortnight,” he says, “and is ready to be shouted through again.” He lays the Greene on the roster. “Today, I’m reliably informed, is the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter. I take it as an endorsement of the method.”
“A load-bearing chair,” Yusuf says, into his coffee.
“Mr. Noorzai has the engineering of it. Rome has been resting a good deal of weight on a chair for some time, and it hasn’t given way yet, much as some of us have kicked at it.”
He gets up, uncaps a marker, and writes it in his tilted hand.

body.text: IS SARAH BOUND BY A VOW SHE MADE TO A GOD SHE DIDN’T BELIEVE IN?

body: “June of ’44,” Hale says, sitting down again. “A flying bomb. The front door comes off its hinges and down on top of Bendrix on the stairs, and Sarah finds him under it, and by every sign she has, he’s dead. So she goes back into the room and kneels on the floor, and she makes an offer to a God she has no grounds whatever to believe in: let him be alive, and she’ll give him up. And in walks Bendrix with plaster in his hair.” He opens his hands over the book. “She keeps it. That isn’t today’s question. Today’s question is whether she has to. The chair, for its part, is a Humean, and holds that a promise to a fiction binds nobody but the fiction. But the chair didn’t write the novel, and the man who did went to Mass. Miss Broussard. The chair.”

Lena answers Hale, not the table, in a voice pitched to reach the middle of the long side and stop there. Hale relays her half a sentence behind, reading it off her as she goes, so Jack gets all of it twice: first her vowels from the window end, low, not quite words at this distance, and then Hale’s, which carry.

“Miss Broussard says yes. She says a promise doesn’t wait until you deserve to have made it. Sarah keeps it because she said it, and keeping it is how she finds out who she said it to.” He checks with the window end. “Miss Broussard calls that the beginning of faith. Not” — another check — “the end of love.” He turns his head the long way round. “Mr. Costigan. The chair is listening, which it doesn’t do for just anybody.”
Yusuf writes something down. The library copy crackles.

Jack’s answer is there before Hale’s head has come back round to the door end. He didn’t have to go looking for it. It was there already, with an edge on it, and it got to the front of him faster than anything he read for today.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. s21.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 22 · 11:10 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE GREEN ONE
body: The Christmas bulbs are down. They’re coiled in a shoebox on the windowsill, and the window over the mattress is just a window now, black, with the surf going at the foot of the bluff behind it. The lamp on the floor makes a low yellow room out of the blanket and the slope of the ceiling. *Brideshead* lies face down by her knee, finished, the Ralphs receipt she has kept her place with since Book Three tucked in after the last page.

She closed it an hour ago without a word about it, and she hasn’t said much since. She lies on her back with her hands folded on her stomach and looks at the ceiling. On the pillowcase under her head the dark rinse has left a faint gray print. Corinne will count it as a wash.
“Where do I buy one?” she says. “A Catechism. The real one. The big one.”
“Borders,” Jack says. “Downtown, on State.”
“Is there a green one? I want the green one.”
His own is white, from his Confirmation, with Father Dom’s signature inside the cover and the spine cracked open at the sacraments. “I don’t know about a green one.”

“At your church. On the table by the water, where you get your fingers wet. Big and green and fat as a phone book, with a card taped on it.” She does the card for him, in the voice of a retired schoolteacher who has been through this before. “*Please don’t take this one.*” She turns her head on the pillow. “I didn’t take it. I *wanted* to. That’s a sin, right? Wanting to take a Catechism?”
“It’s a gray area.”
“Good. I live there.”
Before the white one there was a little blue one, the Baltimore, at St. Brigid’s, with Sister Rose and her whistle. “I know question six,” he says.
“What’s question six?”

“*Why did God make you?* God made me to know Him, to love Him, and to serve Him in this world, and to be happy with Him forever in the next.” It comes out at the speed of a seven-year-old, because that’s the only speed it comes at. “I learned it at seven. I’m still on question six.”

She looks at him a while. Then she rolls off the mattress onto her knees and goes into the carry-on, still not unpacked, and comes back with a motel pen and a page of Dell’s sides, the last one, creased in thirds, her lines in yellow highlighter and her blocking in pencil down the edge. She turns it over to the blank back, puts it on her knee, and writes. He reads it upside down.

body.title: The back of Dell’s last page
body.text:
EUCHARIST

WHY CAN’T HE JUST

body: The pen hangs over the paper after JUST. She doesn’t write the rest. She caps the pen, folds the page in half around it, slides it inside the back cover of *Brideshead*, and leaves the book on the floor by her knee.

She fits herself along his side, her cold feet finding his shins, her head on his shoulder where the gray print will be in the morning, and her breathing slows and lengthens against him, and Jack lies listening to it with the surf coming in under it and can’t think of one thing he wants that isn’t in this room.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Tuesday she booked a pilot: a sheriff’s daughter in a border town who isn’t nice to anybody, outside Santa Fe, sixteen days. I told her Theo asked me to New Orleans. She said go. I told her Friday’s hers. At the red light at Carrillo we sang the whole song at each other, top down, and a girl in the next lane filmed it. She didn’t share it. She wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about Cassidy and her mother and the network. She kissed me and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Thursday she read Danny’s letter out loud, and took my flannel to New Mexico, and left me her sweatshirt. Friday it rained. She said *for now*’s running out of room. I asked her. We fell asleep in each other’s arms. Saturday at six a car took her to New Mexico in the rain, and she left me the Saab. Two weeks as Dell Harlan at seven thousand feet: a motel heater that knocks, the first snow she ever stood in while it fell, a sorrel mare named Clementine who bit the director. Her mother came the second week. Valentine’s, alone, she went to Mass at the cathedral in Santa Fe and found a woe in the Gospel for people everybody likes. She got ashes before call. She came home a day early, to the curb, in the hat, with somebody else’s dark hair. I told her about Wednesdays. Sunday she stayed in the pew with me. Then: explain it to me, until I understand. Monday night she wanted to know where you buy a Catechism. The green one.
